96.opening_line: We should explore using simulation-driven inverse modeling and GNNs to uncover how insurance-claims data are generated.

112.name: Sascha Caron
discussion_points: Can we adapt collider-grade deep generative models (VAEs/GANs with density-information buffers and explicit frequency correction) to accelerate McStas-like neutron transport simulations while preserving rare-tail physics and providing calibrated uncertainty bands—what would the training data, conservation constraints and validation benchmarks look like?

Sascha has used transformer/graph architectures for tracking; could GNNs be repurposed to model complex instrument geometries and sample-environment interactions so we can answer Daniel's core question of "what made the dataset" (e.g., disentangling sample scattering, guide imperfections, and environmental contributions)?

Mixture-of-theories training and ensemble anomaly-detection frameworks have been useful to separate signal hypotheses in collider searches—could that approach be used to jointly infer competing models for instrument backgrounds and sample signals, or to detect unmodelled behaviour in neutron-beamline commissioning?

We could transfer active-learning and high-dimensional optimisation pipelines (used for parameter scans in SUSY and LHC analyses) to cost-sensitive instrument design choices (e.g., piecewise-linear guide shapes for BIFROST) — how would we define acquisition functions that trade simulation cost, manufacturing cost, and physics performance?

There may be cross-domain value in low-latency/neuromorphic benchmarking and online inference: what are the constraints (latency, power, reliability) for deploying neuromorphic or compact GNN-based controllers for realtime beamline diagnostics or ICU-style bedside monitoring, and what experiments could jointly validate them?
112.opening_line: We should compare how collider ML tools—fast generative models, GNNs and uncertainty-aware anomaly detectors—can accelerate and explain neutron-instrument simulations and diagnostics.

26.name: Jerome Chenevez
discussion_points: Neural surrogates for expensive forward simulations: discuss building fast, differentiable emulators (normalizing flows, conditional VAEs, or graph-based surrogates) to replace Monte‑Carlo McStas-style and detector-response runs so we can do gradient-based/inference‑aware parameter searches for instrument/astrophysical models (e.g., fitting reflection or burst‑driven wind models to many simulated detector realizations).

Representing instruments and metadata as graphs: map mirror segments, detector pixels, beamline/sample‑environment elements and spacecraft/experiment telemetry to nodes and edges, then use GNNs to predict data‑quality flags or root causes—this could help separate instrumental artifacts from true astrophysical transients in FITS images/time series and, conversely, diagnose sample‑environment effects in neutron instruments.

Causal/simulation‑based inference to answer 'what made the datasets': explore likelihood‑free methods (neural posterior estimation, sequential neural likelihood) and counterfactual simulations to attribute observed features to physical causes (instrumental configuration, calibration drift, or astrophysical event), with a joint case study such as discriminating burst‑driven spectral lines from detector/systematics.

Cross‑domain transfer of pragmatic engineering approximations: compare the piecewise‑linear guide approximation approach (cost vs performance) used for BIFROST to analogous simplifications in X‑ray optics, mosaicking and spacecraft ground‑system processing, and investigate automated cost/accuracy tradeoff searches (e.g., model compression / pruning analogues for instrument discretization).

A shared ML‑ready benchmark and data‑provenance stack: design a dataset that bundles FITS images/time series, simulated instrument realizations, and telemetry/provenance labels for tasks like surrogate fidelity, anomaly root‑cause attribution, and conditional transient classification—this would give concrete problems for GNNs/NNs beyond LLMs and a testbed for both of our instrumentation needs.
26.opening_line: We should explore simulation‑informed GNNs to link instrument geometry, telemetry, and FITS time series for causal attribution.

87.name: Clément Cherblamc
discussion_points: Hybrid architectures: experiment with coupling GNNs (for irregular meshes/boundaries) and U‑Net super‑resolution (for gridlike fields) to downscale polar regional model outputs into high‑resolution surface mass balance maps — design a training pipeline that enforces mass conservation and ice‑physics constraints and compare to pure grid or pure graph baselines.

Causal‑style generative modeling: build conditional generative models (e.g., physics‑aware VAEs or conditional GANs) that can produce realistic climate forcings or sample‑environment scenarios so we can ask 'what made this dataset' via counterfactuals — apply the same methodology to identify drivers of SMB anomalies and to generate realistic variations of sample environments for neutron simulations.

Surrogate/emulator exchange: use ML surrogates (U‑Nets, GNNs, PINNs) to replace expensive forward simulators — propose a cross‑domain benchmark where Clément provides high‑resolution regional/ice‑sheet outputs and Daniel provides McStas or sample‑environment simulation outputs, then train emulators to accelerate parameter sweeps and uncertainty quantification.

Structured dataset and annotation strategy: co‑design datasets that include explicit, physically meaningful latent factors (forcing indices, boundary conditions, instrument configurations) so ML models can be evaluated not only on prediction error but on ability to recover or be interrogated about the generative factors — this addresses Daniel's goal of understanding 'what made the datasets'.

Cross‑pollination of approximation tactics: compare piecewise linear/geometry simplifications used in neutron guide design with reduced geometric representations in ice‑sheet boundary/bedrock modeling to see how geometric approximation affects ML super‑resolution and simulation fidelity; run a pilot to quantify cost/accuracy tradeoffs and potential manufacturing or computational savings.
87.opening_line: We should explore combining GNNs and U‑Net super‑resolution to build physics‑aware emulators for both ice‑sheet and neutron‑instrument simulations.

49.name: Hans Christiansen
discussion_points: Construct a joint simulation-to-inference pipeline: Hans generates S(q,ω) / spin correlation outputs from strongly correlated models and Daniel feeds these through McStas-like instrument + sample‑environment simulations to create realistic detector data, then train GNNs (or graph+equivariant hybrids) to classify phases or regress microscopic model parameters — discuss architectures, labels, and what ground truth sweeps are most informative.

Model the instrument as a graph: treat neutron guides, choppers, detectors and sample environment as nodes/edges and use GNNs to learn transport properties and sensitivity maps, enabling differentiable, cost‑aware optimization of guide piecewise geometries beyond current piecewise linear approximations.

Bring physics priors into the networks: explore SE(3)/translation/rotation equivariant layers, conservation‑law or sum‑rule constraints, and temperature/detailed‑balance informed losses so that ML respects scattering symmetries and reduces sim‑to‑real gaps when inferring strongly correlated signatures.

Invertibility and causality — what made the dataset?: develop latent generative models (VAEs, normalizing flows, or causal graphs) trained on controlled simulation interventions (disorder, field, temperature, cryostat scattering) to disentangle instrument/systematic effects from intrinsic sample physics and quantify identifiability.

Plan validation, active learning and transfer: design small shared benchmark experiments (e.g., well‑characterized magnetic samples + varying sample environments) to calibrate models, then iterate with active‑learning to select measurements that most reduce model uncertainty; discuss compute, data formats, and metrics for success.
49.opening_line: We should explore training GNNs to recover phases from simulated strongly correlated S(q,ω) passed through realistic neutron‑instrument models.

78.name: Francesca Curbis
discussion_points: How would we construct a graph representation of a full instrument chain—whether a neutron guide plus sample environment or an accelerator beamline with diagnostics—so that nodes/edges encode the right physics (optical elements, scattering centers, mechanical degrees of freedom, detector noise) for GNN‑based inverse design and fault diagnosis?

Could we turn McStas/GENESIS start‑to‑end pipelines into differentiable or fast surrogate models (physics‑informed NNs, normalizing flows, or GNN surrogates) to enable amortized inference of 'what made the dataset'—i.e., infer instrument configuration or sample/environment parameters from measurements?

What are the key differences and commonalities in detector and camera image statistics (neutron position‑sensitive detectors vs MCP/Ce:YAG/CCD beamline images), and can we build physics‑aware denoising, domain‑adaptation, or anomaly‑detection models that transfer across those sensor types if we incorporate sensor noise models explicitly?

Could enforcing physics constraints in graph architectures (phase‑space conservation, flux/energy balance, symmetries) help with interpretable, uncertainty‑aware optimization of engineering tradeoffs—e.g., piecewise linear neutron guides versus manufactured elliptical guides, or undulator taper profiles for FELs?

What would a minimal collaborative benchmark look like for the Oresund region: a small suite of simulated + measured examples (neutron transport through a guide; beam profiles from linac/BPMs) to test GNN surrogates, sim‑to‑real transfer strategies, and causal/inverse‑modeling approaches—what metrics and shared tooling should we prioritize?
78.opening_line: We should explore encoding beamlines and sample environments as graphs to enable inverse, physics‑aware ML across neutron and photon instruments.

95.name: Daniel Alejandro Daza Valdebenito
discussion_points: Can we combine McStas-style neutron/instrument simulators and radiative-transfer forward models (e.g., RADMC-3D) to produce calibrated synthetic protostar/disk observations so autoencoders and siamese nets learn latent variables tied to physical generative parameters (grain-size distribution, accretion rate, instrument misalignment) rather than purely observational features?

Have you considered representing a protoplanetary disk or instrument geometry as a graph (nodes = annuli, grain populations, detectors; edges = transport, scattering, coupling) and using GNNs—similar to transport/geometry problems in instrument simulation—to model dust dynamics or approximate scattering kernels?

Since you are both focused on 'what made the datasets', would simulation-based inference (neural posterior/likelihood estimators, differentiable surrogates) be a promising route to invert instrument-convolved observations and obtain calibrated posteriors on physical parameters, and could we co-develop surrogate models to speed up expensive forward sims?

How could we combine autoencoders and siamese architectures to (a) learn a compact manifold of multi-epoch/multi-wavelength protostellar observations, (b) disentangle instrumental/calibration variations from true astrophysical evolution, and (c) flag anomalous substructures for targeted follow-up?

Given small real-data regimes, which sim-to-real strategies would you prioritize—domain randomization, physics-informed priors, uncertainty-aware/Bayesian DNNs, or active learning—and can instrument simulations be used to generate principled domain shifts for stress-testing transfer and quantifying uncertainty?
95.opening_line: We should explore simulation-informed neural models to uncover the generative physics behind our instruments and protostellar observations.

55.name: Diana Vigah Adetsu
discussion_points: Bridging simulations and field data with calibrated uncertainty: how could Bayesian neural networks and techniques from sim‑to‑real transfer be used to map uncertainty when bringing condensed‑matter simulations (quantum transport, synthetic spectra) into contact with noisy, heterogeneous geophysical measurements like drone‑borne gamma‑ray spectra or EMI?

Spectral‑analysis cross‑fertilization: both of us work with spectra (gamma‑ray spectrometry, ARPES/transport spectral functions). Could we share preprocessing, deconvolution and generative‑model approaches (autoencoders, normalizing flows) to improve peak identification, background subtraction and anomaly detection across domains?

Multimodal sensor fusion and sensor‑hierarchies: Diana’s sensor‑hierarchy for prioritizing EMI/GPR/LiDAR reads like a laboratory experiment plan; can that workflow and associated physics‑informed priors inspire active‑learning strategies for selecting probes (transport vs STM vs ARPES) when mapping phase diagrams in strongly correlated materials, and vice versa?

Unsupervised phase/feature discovery: methods you use for clustering and community detection in spatial data (DBSCAN, MCLUST) might help identify emergent phases in large simulated datasets — could we test these on Hans’s simulated ensembles and Diana’s high‑dimensional field covariates to compare stability, interpretability and sensitivity to noise?

Multiscale sampling and reduced representations: our problems both have multiscale heterogeneity (peat stratigraphy vs electronic correlations). Would ideas from geostatistics (kriging, EBKR, optimal sampling size) or from condensed‑matter multiscale methods (RG, tensor networks) help build compact, physics‑aware surrogates for fast prediction and experiment/survey design?
55.opening_line: We should explore how uncertainty‑aware, multimodal ML pipelines can translate between peatland sensing and phase discovery in correlated materials.

18.name: Noah Al-Khulaifi
discussion_points: Can we use Hans’s quantum-transport and many-body simulators to generate realistic, labeled training data for Noah’s nanowire biosensors (including charge-transport signatures, device noise, and electrode–molecule coupling), and what physical parameters or noise processes must the simulators include so the synthetic data transfers to real experiments?

Methods for unsupervised discovery of phases (e.g., latent-space clustering, spectral embeddings, topological data analysis) have been powerful in strongly correlated systems — could those same approaches reveal hidden molecular conformations, binding substates, or rare event kinetics in single-molecule image stacks and time traces, and what pre-processing (drift correction, normalization) would be required?

Physics‑informed and generative models (PINNs, VAEs/normalizing flows, diffusion models) can impose conservation laws or known device physics while denoising or performing deconvolution: how feasible is it to combine a device-level forward model of nanowire conductance with ML-based inverse solvers to extract binding kinetics or spatial localization from low SNR signals?

Active-learning and experiment-design strategies used in simulation-driven condensed-matter studies (e.g., Bayesian optimization over control parameters) could be applied to choose bias voltages, sampling rates, illumination, or microscope settings in real time to maximize detection of single-molecule events — what metrics of information gain would be meaningful for Noah’s experiments and how would we close the loop experimentally?

Practically, what common tooling and benchmarks could we build to enable collaboration — e.g., a shared repo that converts condensed-matter simulator outputs (Kwant/NEGF, model Hamiltonians) into microscope/sensor-like data formats, plus a set of annotated experimental traces from Noah for domain-adaptation tests; who would manage labeling, compute, and versioning?
18.opening_line: We should explore how simulation-driven ML from quantum transport could accelerate robust signal extraction and state discovery in nanowire single‑molecule biosensing.

36.name: Dmitry Baranov
discussion_points: Can we pretrain transformer architectures on simulated strongly‑correlated/quantum‑transport time dynamics (Hubbard, Frenkel‑Holstein, exciton‑polaron models) and fine‑tune them on Dmitry’s pump‑probe and time‑resolved scattering datasets to recover microscopic parameters (couplings, disorder, polaron formation, carrier lifetimes)?

Could we use conditional generative models (diffusion models / VAEs) to propose ligand chemistries or polymer‑encapsulation recipes that optimize stability and suppress halide segregation, and run a closed loop where Dmitry’s rapid synthesis and stability assays provide labels for active learning?

What if we represent superlattices/supercrystals as graphs (nodes = nanocrystals or nanoplatelets, edges = ligand‑mediated couplings) and train GNNs to predict emergent optical/transport properties (superradiance strength, PL shifts, carrier mobility) using inputs from multilayer diffraction, TEM, and simulated transport metrics from Hans’ models?

Can Hans generate targeted simulated scattering and transport fingerprints for specific correlated‑disorder scenarios so we can train inverse‑models to map X‑ray multilayer diffraction / scattering patterns to spatial defect maps and correlated phase indicators in perovskite assemblies?

How do we best incorporate physics priors (sum rules, conservation laws, rate‑equation structure, DFT energetics) into transformers/generative models to improve interpretability and design experiments (specific pump–probe delays, temperatures, doping) that disentangle single‑particle vs correlated many‑body signatures in the experimental observables?
36.opening_line: We should combine simulated strongly‑correlated dynamics with transformer, generative, and graph models to interpret ultrafast spectra and suggest more stable perovskite assemblies.

12.name: Thomas Berlok
discussion_points: Unsupervised discovery of transitions: Could we adapt tools used to find emergent order‑parameters in strongly correlated electron systems (diffusion maps, VAEs, contrastive learning) to identify precursors and low‑dimensional diagnostics of critical transitions in plasma simulations — e.g., the MTI quench when heat flux is microscopically suppressed? What specific observables (magnetic topology metrics, heat‑flux moments, kurtosis of distribution functions) should we feed into such algorithms?

ML closures and emulators for microphysics: Hans' experience with simulated condensed‑matter data could help train ML surrogates that map high‑resolution Vlasov/particle kinetics to effective transport closures (anisotropic viscosity, suppressed conductivity) for MHD codes (Arepo, Paicos). What training strategies (supervised regression, physics‑informed NNs, operator learning) and loss functions (conservation constraints, invariants) would make such closures stable and transferable across regimes?

Phase‑space compression with many‑body methods: Can techniques from many‑body/strongly correlated physics (tensor networks, low‑rank factorization) or ML approaches developed for electronic structure be repurposed to compress high‑dimensional kinetic phase‑space data and to expose long‑range correlations (e.g., trapped particle beams, phase‑space holes) in turbulent plasmas? Would that enable longer, cheaper kinetic simulations or new diagnostics?

Generative models and synthetic diagnostics: How can normalizing flows / diffusion models be used to generate realistic particle distribution functions and synthetic observables (emission maps, line profiles) so we can do domain adaptation between simulations and telescope/experimental data? Could we jointly train models to invert noisy observations back to constrained microphysical states with calibrated uncertainties?

Symmetry/structure‑preserving ML and transferability: Both MHD/kinetic plasma systems and condensed‑matter lattices have strong symmetry and conservation constraints — can equivariant GNNs or Hamiltonian/port‑Hamiltonian networks provide the right inductive bias? Let's discuss concrete architectures and validation tests (energy conservation over long rolls, correct dispersion relations) that would convince domain scientists to adopt ML in production HPC workflows.
12.opening_line: Shall we explore how ML approaches for finding emergent order in correlated electrons could help parameterize microphysical closures in astrophysical plasma simulations?

11.name: Jonas Berx
discussion_points: GFlowNets for topology-aware sampling: could we design reward functions and state representations so a GFlowNet trained on simulated polymer data preferentially generates knotted configurations with controlled knot type and geometric embedding, and then transfer those sampling strategies to explore topological sectors of many-body lattice states (e.g., flux/loop configurations in correlated models)?

Braid groups and Jones polynomials as cross-domain descriptors: can the braid/circuit-topology measures Jonas uses for multichain entanglement be computed on simulated current-loop or worldline configurations in correlated-electron simulations, and could Hans map those invariants to observable transport signatures (conductance fluctuations, shot noise) that distinguish topological/entangled phases?

BLUES and nonlinear solver acceleration for many-body transport: might the BLUES analytic-iteration and convergence-acceleration techniques be adapted to speed up self-consistent solvers used in DMFT/non-equilibrium Green’s functions or nonlinear PDEs appearing in quantum transport models, reducing computational cost for parameter scans needed to generate ML training data?

Thermodynamic/information bounds in quantum transport: how transferable are the stochastic-thermodynamics trade-offs and Fano-factor bounds from soft-matter/non-equilibrium systems to electron transport in strongly correlated systems, and can simulated transport data be used to test Pareto fronts relating dissipation, information flow, and detectability of topological order?

Shared benchmark dataset and evaluation: could we co-design a simulated dataset—knotted polymer conformations coupled to simple electron-transport models (molecular junctions or toy lattice Hamiltonians)—to benchmark topology-aware generative samplers (GFlowNets) and classifiers, with clearly defined evaluation metrics that connect topology labels to measurable transport observables?
11.opening_line: We should explore how knot-theoretic descriptors and GFlowNet sampling can link polymer topology to transport signatures and phases in simulated correlated systems.

97.name: Christian Bierlich
discussion_points: Compare PYTHIA's modular string-based mechanisms (string shoving, rope hadronization, colour reconnection) with microscopic models that produce collective behaviour in strongly correlated electron systems — could a set of local, physically motivated interaction rules reproduce emergent phases or transport anomalies in lattice/quantum-transport simulations?

Explore adapting normalizing flows and HOMER-style generative models used for hadronization to learn many-body objects in condensed matter (spectral functions, reduced density matrices, variational wavefunctions): which physical constraints (sum rules, causality, global symmetries) and architectures would be critical to preserve for reliable extrapolation?

Translate uncertainty-aware reweighting and automated fragmentation-variation techniques from event-generator systematics to condensed-matter parameter studies (disorder realizations, interaction strength, temperature): can reweighting produce fast, rigorous error bands for simulated transport/STM/PES observables and help bridge simulation to experimental imaging?

Propose a cross-domain benchmark/dataset (in the spirit of MLHAD/ML datasets) for non-equilibrium transport: a compact, open simulated suite (time-resolved currents, local correlators, spectral data) and a task list (phase classification, DOS reconstruction, surrogate modeling) with shared metrics — what minimal formats and metrics would make this most useful to both communities?

Discuss building a hybrid pipeline analogous to PYTHIA+UrQMD for condensed matter: couple a microscopic scattering/event generator to a mesoscale transport solver (e.g., Boltzmann/kinetic or Lindblad dynamics) and accelerate parts with ML surrogates — what fidelity, coupling strategies, and computational resources would be needed for a proof-of-principle?
97.opening_line: We should explore whether PYTHIA-style generative Monte Carlo can help simulate strongly correlated electron transport.

105.name: Jack Bodine
discussion_points: Designing physics-aware augmentations: discuss concrete augmentation strategies that respect symmetries and conservation laws (e.g., translational/rotational equivariance, particle–hole symmetry, instrument noise models) so U‑nets trained on simulated condensed‑matter or plasma images generalize to real experimental data.

Sim‑to‑real transfer for phase identification: pick specific simulated observables (STM topographs, spectral function maps, local conductance, or plasma camera frames) that Hans can generate and Jack can use to train segmentation/classification networks, then evaluate domain‑adaptation methods (adversarial adaptation, cycleGANs, physics‑informed losses) for bridging to real measurements.

Spatial pattern segmentation across domains: explore applying U‑net segmentation to analogous structures — Mott/charge‑order domains, domain walls, and filamentary plasma structures — and define useful labels/metrics (domain boundaries, defect types, percolation pathways) that are meaningful to both condensed‑matter and plasma diagnostics.

Active learning and experiment design: develop an uncertainty‑driven acquisition pipeline where models trained on simulated data suggest the most informative experimental probes or scan locations (STM points, transport parameter sweeps, or high‑speed camera frames) to accelerate discovery of new phases or transient plasma phenomena.

Feasible short collaborative projects and career transition steps: outline 2–3 small, high‑impact deliverables Jack could lead (e.g., benchmark of augmentation strategies on simulated→real STM data; U‑net pipeline to segment IEC fusion camera frames; a reproducible sim→segmentation tutorial), including datasets, timeframes, and authorship expectations to help Jack move from CS into physics research.
105.opening_line: Let's explore how U‑net segmentation and physics‑driven simulated data can jointly reveal hidden structures in both plasma diagnostics and strongly correlated materials.

71.name: Raphael Bonnet Guerrini
discussion_points: How can interpretable ML methods (e.g., symbolic regression, concept bottlenecks, sparse rule learners) be adapted to extract physically meaningful order parameters or emergent quasiparticle descriptions from simulated strongly correlated-electron datasets, and could the same interpretable probes be applied to identify signatures of neutrino or supernova events in detector time-series?

Which sim‑to‑real strategies (normalizing flows/emulators, domain adversarial training, likelihood‑free inference) have you found most effective for moving models trained on simulated condensed‑matter or particle‑physics data to real experiments, and can we design a cross‑domain benchmark (phase‑boundary recovery vs particle/signal classification) to compare them systematically?

Could causal inference or invariant representation learning help disentangle instrument/systematic effects from true physical signals both in LHC/neutrino searches and in quantum transport experiments, and might Bayesian fine‑mapping/prioritization ideas from genomics aid in ranking candidate mechanisms or defects?

Are there shared low‑dimensional representations or signatures learned by graph/latent‑space models that capture collective excitations in correlated materials and collective phenomena in high‑energy cascades, and how can interpretable probes read out physically meaningful variables from those representations?

Can we combine uncertainty‑aware interpretable surrogates with active experimental design—using simulated data to propose the next optimal measurement (energy scans, ARPES angles, detector triggers)—so experiments are both information‑efficient and produce results that physicists can transparently act on?
71.opening_line: We should explore interpretable ML tools that can reveal emergent physics across strongly correlated materials simulations and neutrino/LHC detector data.

79.name: Hippolyte Bourel
discussion_points: How would we map the experimental control/measurement loop in quantum-transport or strongly correlated materials to a model-based RL MDP/average-reward setup—what are the natural states, actions, reset costs and per-step rewards in your lab measurements, and are experiment durations better modeled as continuing (average-reward) or episodic trials?

Can we exploit known physical symmetries, order parameters or conserved quantities as the 'equivalence classes' that Hippolyte's ApproxEquivalence/C-UCRL uses to reduce exploration? If those are incomplete, would Hans's simulators/measurements provide enough signal to discover emergent equivalence classes (phases) experimentally?

Many correlated systems show hysteresis, slow relaxation and history dependence—could we formalize those as non‑Markovian reward machines (high‑level automata) so RL algorithms learn policies that respect memory effects (e.g., path-dependent phase switching) rather than being misled by Markov assumptions?

Given Hans uses simulated data, can we design a sim-to-real curriculum where variance-aware, time-uniform concentration and regret bounds guide how much to trust simulation pretraining vs. costly real experiments—what is the typical simulator fidelity and noise model, and how costly are physical measurements per sample?

What infrastructure and acceptance barriers exist for closed‑loop experimental automation in your condensed-matter setups, and how could interpretable policy structure (equivalence classes, reward machines) make automated decisions and results more trustworthy to experimentalists and enable shared datasets for benchmarking?
79.opening_line: We should explore applying equivalence-aware, model-based RL and non‑Markovian reward structure to accelerate discovering phases in strongly correlated materials.

115.name: Jan-Matthias Braun
discussion_points: Explore using FPGA‑friendly reservoir computing / echo‑state networks (given Jan‑Matthias’s HLS toolchains) to emulate non‑equilibrium dynamics from Hans’s simulated quantum‑transport datasets, enabling orders‑of‑magnitude faster sweeps of parameter space when searching for new phases.

Apply physics‑informed neural networks to inverse problems in condensed matter: embed conservation laws or approximate Hamiltonian structure (ideas from plasma / nonlinear systems) to infer effective models or scattering potentials directly from transport or spectroscopy traces.

Translate chaos diagnostics (Lyapunov spectra, finite‑time entropy rates, recurrence quantification) used in plasma and nonlinear systems to characterize thermalization vs. many‑body localization in strongly correlated electron simulations, and test whether these metrics predict phase boundaries more robustly than standard order parameters.

Adapt explainable‑AI and clinically motivated interpretability pipelines (saliency, counterfactuals, concept activation, and low‑dimensional autoencoder visualizations) developed for biomedical imaging to make unsupervised / generative model discoveries of novel phases physically interpretable and experimentally testable.

Prototype a transfer pipeline from simulated data to low‑power, real‑time edge inference: discuss data augmentation and domain‑adaptation strategies so models trained on Hans’s simulated condensed‑matter data can be deployed on Jan‑style embedded hardware for in‑lab, closed‑loop control or online classification during transport experiments.
115.opening_line: We could explore combining low‑power, physics‑informed neural hardware with simulated quantum‑transport data to speed discovery of correlated phases.

69.name: Nuno Brás
discussion_points: Compare the forward/inverse scattering math in corneal optics (radiative transfer, Mie/phase-function models, multiple scattering) with electron/quantum transport formalisms (Green’s functions, Boltzmann/quantum kinetic equations, Anderson localization): could we adapt corneal forward‑models to produce synthetic quantum‑transport observables or, conversely, borrow numerical solvers from condensed matter to make more realistic corneal scattering simulators for ML training?

Explore using score‑based/diffusion generative models as posterior samplers for ill‑posed inverse problems in both fields — e.g., reconstructing spatial refractive‑index maps of the cornea or latent many‑body states from noisy transport/spectroscopy data — and explicitly inject physics constraints (symmetries, conservation laws, reciprocity) into the reverse diffusion dynamics.

Translate U‑Net + super‑resolution and adversarial denoising pipelines across domains: can architectures and loss functions that improve OCT/corneal layer segmentation and super‑resolution be repurposed for denoising/enhancing STM, TEM or simulated spectroscopy images, and can domain‑adaptation from simulated quantum data improve robustness of ophthalmic models to rare scattering regimes?

Joint interpretability and latent‑variable discovery: develop physics‑aware representation learning (disentangling correlation length, scatterer size distribution, interaction strength) so latent units map to measurable physical quantities in both corneal transparency and strongly correlated materials; evaluate with targeted interventions on simulators and with concept‑level attribution (e.g., sensitivity of transport coefficients or diagnostic indices).

Build a shared simulator‑to‑ML benchmarking pipeline and uncertainty quantification stack: combine high‑fidelity forward simulators (photon and electron scattering solvers) with amortized/likelihood‑free inference (conditional diffusion, normalizing flows, Bayesian surrogates) to compare reconstruction accuracy, calibration, and computational cost — an opportunity for a cross‑disciplinary open dataset and reproducible benchmark.
69.opening_line: We should explore whether diffusion models and physics‑informed U‑Nets for corneal scattering can inform inverse problems in quantum transport.

27.name: Pietro Butti
discussion_points: Try a cross-disciplinary pipeline: train convolutional/graph autoencoders on lattice QFT Monte‑Carlo configurations to extract condensates or topological features, then apply the same pipeline to simulated Hubbard/t‑J snapshots to see if the learned latent coordinates map to known order parameters (Mott gap, spin/charge order) — this could reveal universal latent representations and a route to interpretable order‑parameter discovery.

Develop and compare RG‑inspired latent dynamics: use neural ODEs / stochastic neural ODEs to learn coarse‑graining flows from high‑resolution Monte‑Carlo or exact‑diagonalization data, and test whether the learned flows reproduce known renormalization group fixed points in both lattice gauge models and condensed‑matter models (e.g., 2D Ising, lattice gauge Higgs, Hubbard), thereby probing universality and transferability of ML‑learned RG maps.

Collaborate on non‑equilibrium transport and contagion analogies: adapt Pietro’s percolation/RG models and stochastic latent dynamics to model thermalization and quantum transport after quenches in strongly correlated systems, and conversely use quantum transport simulations (Kubo, NEGF) to inform epidemic‑style models of spreading on networks — exploring shared metrics (susceptibility, conductivity, percolation thresholds) and data‑driven reduced descriptions.

Bring physics constraints into ML for translational imaging and simulation: design gauge‑equivariant/fermion‑aware normalizing flows or symmetry‑preserving autoencoders that both accelerate Monte‑Carlo sampling for sign‑problem‑prone fermionic systems and regularize latent predictors for PSMA‑PET/radiotherapy response, creating a pipeline that fuses simulated transport physics with clinical imaging biomarkers.

Set up a shared benchmark and validation protocol that addresses interpretability and hard limits: define tasks (order‑parameter recovery, sampling acceleration, predicting transport coefficients, forecasting treatment response), include simulated datasets (lattice gauge ensembles, Hubbard snapshots, transport outputs), and evaluate performance with physics‑aware metrics (conservation laws, symmetry‑respect, fidelity of condensate values) to make results reproducible and comparable across our fields.
27.opening_line: We should compare how autoencoders, normalizing flows, and neural ODEs can reveal emergent degrees of freedom across lattice gauge theory and strongly correlated electron systems.

96.name: William Bærenholdt
discussion_points: Strong correlations as a shared problem: compare methods used for strongly correlated electrons (e.g., tensor networks, DMFT, variational many-body methods) with approaches to model dependence between insurance lines and large losses—could tensor-factorization or physics-inspired low-rank approximations capture high-order claim dependencies and tail co-movements?

Phase transitions versus systemic risk: discuss borrowing unsupervised and topological techniques from physics (order-parameter discovery, clustering across scales, persistent homology) to detect regime changes or emerging systemic events in claims time series and portfolios—what would an "early-warning" order parameter for insurance look like?

Simulated data and synthetic-tail generation: Hans works with simulators; William has scarce tail events—could physics-style simulators or generative models (diffusion/GANs conditioned on actuarial priors) be used to create calibrated synthetic claims for stress-testing ML models, and how would we validate/regularize those simulants to satisfy regulators?

Interpretable, uncertainty-aware ML across domains: both fields need robust uncertainty quantification—explore translating Bayesian hierarchical models, principled OOD detection, and causal/structural priors from physics to build explainable risk scores (e.g., CVaR-aware predictors) that provide scientifically interpretable explanations for high-loss predictions.

Multi-scale/renormalization analogies and architectures: probe the conceptual parallel between renormalization/coarse-graining in condensed matter and aggregating micro-level claims into macro risk metrics—could multi-scale neural architectures or coarse-graining algorithms improve aggregation, calibration, and transferability of models across portfolios and time horizons?
96.opening_line: We should explore whether tools for finding emergent phases in physics can help reveal emergent systemic risks in insurance claims.

112.name: Sascha Caron
discussion_points: How might Sascha’s deep generative models with a density‑information buffer be adapted to produce high‑fidelity synthetic many‑body observables (spectral functions, STM/ARPES images, conductance traces) conditioned on Hamiltonian parameters, and what metrics would we use to ensure ‘frequency‑correct’ physical realism for condensed‑matter use cases?

Could the DeepXS paradigm — an ultra‑fast surrogate for expensive NLO cross‑section evaluations — be translated into a ‘DeepManyBody’ that maps Hamiltonian or control‑parameter space to target observables (e.g., Green’s functions, gap magnitudes, transport coefficients), and how should we combine active learning and uncertainty quantification to train it using costly DMRG/QMC simulations?

Sascha’s anomaly‑detection toolchain (ensemble One‑Class DSVD + flows, DDD, mixture‑of‑theories training) has proved useful for model‑independent search at the LHC — can similar frameworks detect emergent/rare phases or precursors to phase transitions in large simulated or experimental condensed‑matter datasets, and what would constitute a physically meaningful validation pipeline for such ‘anomalies’?

Transformer and graph architectures developed for tracking and event classification might map naturally onto lattice geometries, time‑dependent correlation sequences, or quantum transport channel graphs — what representation (node/edge features, sequence tokens) and pretraining tasks would most effectively transfer collider ML advances to strongly correlated electron problems?

Given the value of large public benchmarks (Dark Machines) and tools like SPOT/AutoSourceID, should we design an open, uncertainty‑aware benchmark suite for condensed‑matter ML (synthetic many‑body events, STM/ARPES/transport traces, labelled phase maps) that includes energy/latency targets for neuromorphic or in‑lab deployment, and what minimal dataset/metadata standards would we require?
112.opening_line: We should explore whether collider‑grade generative and anomaly‑detection tools can accelerate uncertainty‑aware discovery of phases in strongly correlated materials.

26.name: Jerome Chenevez
discussion_points: Sim2real and domain adaptation: use Hans's simulated strongly‑correlated / quantum‑transport data to develop transfer‑learning pipelines for Jerome's FITS time‑series and X‑ray images (e.g., train on labeled simulations with realistic instrument noise models from INTEGRAL/NuSTAR/JEM‑X, then adapt to real bursts, QPOs, and transient detections). What kinds of degradation/noise models and evaluation metrics would make a fair sim→real benchmark for both fields?

Discovering ‘phases’ and transitions across domains: apply unsupervised representation learning (contrastive learning, VAEs, clustering) to Jerome's catalogs (MINBAR, long/intermediate bursts, accretion states) and Hans's simulated phase diagrams to ask whether accretion states or burst‑driven winds behave like phase transitions in correlated systems — can techniques for identifying electronic phases help classify accretion regimes and vice versa?

Graph‑based spectral‑timing models: represent energy channels, spectral components, or detector networks as graphs and apply GNN architectures used for lattice/transport problems to model energy‑dependent phase lags, spectral line propagation, and reflection timing signatures; could graph representations expose causal links between disk, corona, and burst signals?

Physics‑informed surrogates and inverse problems: build differentiable, physics‑constrained ML surrogates (e.g., normalizing‑flow posteriors, neural surrogates of radiative transfer/reflection models) trained on controlled condensed‑matter/astrophysical simulations to accelerate parameter inference for cyclotron lines, disk inner‑radius, and burst–disk interaction — how to best encode domain priors and quantify epistemic/aleatoric uncertainty in low‑S/N regimes?

Joint benchmark datasets and a hackathon-style challenge: design a shared, versioned dataset (FITS + simulated data) with injected labeled phenomena — QPOs, mHz oscillations, bursts, reflection features, transient counterparts — to compare anomaly detection, change‑point detection, and phase‑discovery methods from both communities; propose a short collaborative event where Jerome supplies realistic FITS catalogs/instrument models and Hans supplies simulated ground‑truth datasets and evaluation pipelines.
26.opening_line: Let's explore physics‑aware ML that bridges simulated quantum‑transport data and FITS X‑ray time series.

87.name: Clément Cherblamc
discussion_points: Can we adapt U‑Net style super‑resolution used for climate fields to ‘upscale’ coarse many‑body simulation outputs (e.g., momentum‑space spectral functions or local observables) — what representation (real‑space grid, lattice graph, or k‑space) and loss functions best preserve the relevant physics?

What are principled ways to inject physics constraints that both of us care about — mass/energy conservation and boundary fluxes for polar surface mass balance versus particle number, charge conservation, and lattice symmetries in strongly correlated systems — e.g., via equivariant layers, constrained decoders, or physics‑informed priors?

How can generative models and Bayesian pipelines (flows, diffusion models, SBI) be used to produce realistic ensembles and quantify uncertainty in regimes that lack observations — extreme melt events for ice sheets and rare emergent phases/transport regimes in correlated materials — and what validation strategies can cross‑fertilize our fields?

Could unsupervised representation learning or topology‑aware latent spaces reveal new ‘phases’ in both domains — for instance, melt‑feedback regimes or tipping behavior in polar climates and novel order parameters or hidden phases in correlated electron systems — and what diagnostics would make such discoveries credible to domain experts?

On the practical side, where do our computational bottlenecks and data formats align? Would a joint benchmark — e.g., super‑resolving coarse model outputs to high‑resolution fields/observables with physically constrained U‑Nets, plus transfer‑learning experiments between simulated and observational/experimental data — be a productive first project, and which open tools (xarray/NetCDF, PyTorch equivariant libs) should we standardize on?
87.opening_line: We should compare physics‑aware super‑resolution and generative ML strategies to reveal fine‑scale structure in ice‑sheet mass balance and correlated‑electron systems.

31.name: Daniel Lomholt Christensen
discussion_points: Construct a joint simulation-to-inference pipeline: Hans generates S(q,ω) / spin correlation outputs from strongly correlated models and Daniel feeds these through McStas-like instrument + sample‑environment simulations to create realistic detector data, then train GNNs (or graph+equivariant hybrids) to classify phases or regress microscopic model parameters — discuss architectures, labels, and what ground truth sweeps are most informative.

Model the instrument as a graph: treat neutron guides, choppers, detectors and sample environment as nodes/edges and use GNNs to learn transport properties and sensitivity maps, enabling differentiable, cost‑aware optimization of guide piecewise geometries beyond current piecewise linear approximations.

Bring physics priors into the networks: explore SE(3)/translation/rotation equivariant layers, conservation‑law or sum‑rule constraints, and temperature/detailed‑balance informed losses so that ML respects scattering symmetries and reduces sim‑to‑real gaps when inferring strongly correlated signatures.

Invertibility and causality — what made the dataset?: develop latent generative models (VAEs, normalizing flows, or causal graphs) trained on controlled simulation interventions (disorder, field, temperature, cryostat scattering) to disentangle instrument/systematic effects from intrinsic sample physics and quantify identifiability.

Plan validation, active learning and transfer: design small shared benchmark experiments (e.g., well‑characterized magnetic samples + varying sample environments) to calibrate models, then iterate with active‑learning to select measurements that most reduce model uncertainty; discuss compute, data formats, and metrics for success.
31.opening_line: We should explore training GNNs to recover phases from simulated strongly correlated S(q,ω) passed through realistic neutron‑instrument models.

78.name: Francesca Curbis
discussion_points: Sim-to-real transfer: compare challenges in moving from high-fidelity beamline/accelerator simulations to real diagnostics (images, monitors) with Hans's simulated data for strongly correlated systems—could we co-develop physics-aware domain adaptation (cycleGAN/physics-constrained flows, domain-adversarial training) and a joint benchmark to quantify sim-to-real gaps?

Surrogate/emulator strategies for costly forward models: exchange approaches for building fast ML emulators of GENESIS/beam-dynamics and of many‑body solvers (DMRG/DMFT/QMC), including uncertainty quantification (deep ensembles, Bayesian NNs) and active learning for targeted parameter scans to reduce expensive simulations on both sides.

Real‑time tuning and control: explore adapting RL/optimal-control approaches used for online accelerator tuning (beam steering, bunch compression) to laboratory control problems in quantum-transport experiments (gate voltages, temperature, drive pulses) and conversely bring precision control ideas from condensed-matter to improve automated beamline stabilization.

Coherence and spectral diagnostics as a shared language: discuss methods Francesca uses to characterize temporal/spectral coherence in FEL pulses (phase retrieval, coherence metrics) and whether analogous signal-processing/ML tools could reveal emergent coherence or subtle spectral signatures of new phases in transport and spectroscopic data (ARPES, optical conductivity).

Imaging and end-to-end pipelines: identify a concrete pilot—use MAX IV imaging/ptychography or soft X‑ray beamlines to probe candidate correlated materials and co-design ML pipelines (denoising, reconstruction, anomaly/phase classification) leveraging Francesca's diagnostics data formats and Hans's physics priors to accelerate discovery.
78.opening_line: Let's explore how our simulation-driven ML for beam diagnostics and many‑body materials can cross‑pollinate to speed discovery, control, and coherence detection.

95.name: Daniel Alejandro Daza Valdebenito
discussion_points: Autoencoders as physics‑aware compressors: could we train autoencoders on radiative‑transfer simulations of protoplanetary disks (conditioned on grain size, turbulence, inclination) to produce low‑dimensional, interpretable latents — and can Hans' experience with volumetric imaging pipelines and simulated data help design loss terms or regularizers that enforce radiative/energy conservation or known scaling laws?

Siamese/contrastive networks for temporal matching and proper‑motion inference: can we use Siamese architectures to match substructures across multi‑epoch or multiwavelength observations (detecting migrating clumps or evolving rings), borrowing ideas from contrastive representations used in other tracking problems and from Hans' image‑fusion registration workflows to robustly register and compare observations?

Simulation→real domain adaptation and calibrated uncertainty: how can we combine deep networks with Bayesian recalibration (PAINTOR‑style or hierarchical Bayesian posteriors) so that parameter estimates from models trained on simulations have trustworthy error bars on real telescope data — and could Hans' experience with Bayesian prioritization and causal‑variant calibration inform strategy for posterior correction and priors?

Generative benchmarks and community datasets: would it be productive to co‑develop an open, annotated suite of simulated disk images (varying dust physics, substructure types, noise/PSF) using conditional generative models, plus an open pipeline for fusing multiwavelength stacks (inspired by Hans' 3D Slicer workflow), so experimentalists and ML newcomers (like Daniel) have standard training/validation sets?

Unsupervised discovery of ‘phases’ or morphology classes: can unsupervised manifold learning, clustering in latent space, or topological data analysis—techniques used to find phases in strongly correlated systems—be adapted to automatically discover and interpret disk substructure classes (rings vs spirals vs vortices), and how would we link latent features back to physical quantities such as dust‑to‑gas ratio or local turbulence?
95.opening_line: We should explore how simulation‑trained deep models plus Bayesian prioritization can connect protoplanetary‑disk imaging and condensed‑matter inference.

55.name: Diana Vigah Adetsu
discussion_points: Bayesian uncertainty for detector calibration: explore applying Diana’s Bayesian neural‑network workflows to accelerator imaging and detector diagnostics (MCPs, Ce:YAG cameras, spectrometers) to produce well‑calibrated uncertainties for photon/particle counts and, conversely, adapt accelerator image‑calibration techniques to improve energy/background correction for drone‑borne and ground gamma‑ray spectrometers.

Real‑time, edge ML for streaming instruments: compare constraints and solutions for on‑the‑fly inference — lightweight NNs, pruning/quantization, and online updating — for drone‑based GR/EMI surveys and low‑latency beamline feedback (timing overlap, intensity monitors), and consider building a common benchmark for throughput/latency vs accuracy.

Sensor‑hierarchies and multimodal fusion: test the transfer of Diana’s sensor‑hierarchy and fusion rules (EMI, GPR, LiDAR, GR) into accelerator diagnostics (fast coarse monitors + high‑resolution spectrometers) and reciprocally use multi‑diagnostic fusion strategies from FEL work to improve peat thickness/suitability maps and GPR sampling planning.

Unsupervised anomaly detection and temporal drift: evaluate clustering and density methods you both use (DBSCAN, MCLUST, ensemble clustering) for cross‑domain anomaly detection — e.g., identifying beamline instabilities or detector faults vs localized subsidence or sudden changes in peat properties — and develop drift‑aware pipelines for long‑term monitoring.

Simulation‑informed ML and optimal sampling: leverage start‑to‑end accelerator simulation experience and geophysical forward models to produce synthetic training sets, then co‑develop active‑learning/optimal‑design strategies for where to place sensors or take high‑cost measurements (drone transects vs beamline diagnostics) to maximize information per measurement.
55.opening_line: We should explore how uncertainty‑aware ML and lightweight diagnostics could link peatland geophysics and FEL instrumentation.

18.name: Noah Al-Khulaifi
discussion_points: Low‑SNR transient event detection as a shared problem: compare signal‑processing baselines (matched filters, wavelets) with modern ML options (1D/2D CNNs, temporal convolution, transformer or RNN-based sequence models) for detecting single‑molecule hits in nanowires versus short‑lived beam/shot features in accelerator images; discuss creating a small joint benchmark dataset and evaluation metrics that reflect both false‑alarm cost and missed‑event risk.

Simulation‑to‑real (sim2real) transfer and synthetic data pipelines: both groups rely on forward simulators (GENESIS/beamline start‑to‑end for FELs; physics‑based models for nanowire sensors). Explore building differentiable forward models or domain‑randomized synthetic training sets, and compare domain‑adaptation strategies (CycleGAN, feature‑space alignment, physics‑informed losses) to reduce labeling needs.

Real‑time inference and closed‑loop control requirements: contrast latency, model‑size and reliability constraints for online beamline feedback (FPGA/CPU constraints, safety) with requirements for near‑real‑time biosensing analysis; discuss model compression/pruning, quantization, and architectures amenable to embedded deployment so ML can be integrated into control loops in both labs.

Uncertainty quantification and interpretability for experiment‑critical decisions: discuss approaches (Bayesian NNs, deep ensembles, MC dropout, conformal prediction) to produce calibrated uncertainties for single‑event detections and accelerator diagnostics, and exchange ideas about visual/explainable outputs that experimentalists trust when deciding to trigger downstream actions.

Cross‑fertilization of diagnostics and instrumentation techniques: investigate whether accelerator imaging/diagnostics tools (e.g., MCP/Ce:YAG BPM characterization, spectrometer image denoising) can be adapted to improve nanowire sensor readout, and whether single‑molecule localization/denoising and sparse‑event detection algorithms developed in biophysics could help pick out transient microbunching or seeding signatures in FEL data — propose a small pilot project to test one algorithm on each other's datasets.
18.opening_line: We should compare how low‑SNR transient images in nanowire biosensing and accelerator diagnostics drive different ML strategies.

36.name: Dmitry Baranov
discussion_points: Time‑zero and jitter correction for ultrafast pump‑probe at FELs: discuss applying Francesca’s timing/overlap diagnostics and transformer/time‑series ML models to learn per‑shot timing offsets from beamline monitors (Ce:YAG/BPMs, MCPs) and correct Dmitry’s pump‑probe and 2D spectroscopy traces in real time to recover sub‑50 fs structure in colloidal perovskite measurements.

Transfering beam‑diagnostics image workflows to materials characterization: explore porting convolutional/transformer models and unsupervised anomaly detectors used for beam profile, spectrometer and BPM images to automate analysis of TEM/SEM, X‑ray scattering CCDs and multilayer‑diffraction maps — e.g., rapid identification of halide segregation, superlattice disorder, or aging signatures from scattering frames.

Graph/transformer representations linking structure → exciton transport → optics: propose building graph models of ligand‑bound nanoplatelet/superlattice connectivity (nodes = nanocrystals, ligands, interfaces; edges = coupling or separation) and training graph‑transformers to predict PL shifts, energy transfer rates or superradiant behavior; Francesca’s experience modelling component networks and wakefield coupling could guide priors for propagation/stability in these graphs.

Generative models and active learning for synthesis and encapsulation: consider diffusion/graph generative models to propose ligand chemistries or polymer capsule formulations that improve aqueous/photostability, combined with an active‑learning loop that proposes experiments and uses rapid beamline/spectroscopic readout (with online ML scoring) to close the loop and prioritize promising candidates.

Designing joint FEL/beamline experiments with ML‑based damage control and surrogate modelling: plan collaborative experiments at MAX IV (or FEL beamlines) on perovskite supercrystals where ML surrogate models predict damage thresholds and spectral yield per pulse, and an online optimizer (Bayesian/REINFORCE or model‑based control) tunes pulse energy, repetition rate and focus to maximize useful signal while minimizing sample degradation.
36.opening_line: We should combine accelerator timing, ML and perovskite ultrafast probes to enable damage‑aware, high‑throughput experiments.

12.name: Thomas Berlok
discussion_points: Can we adapt the image‑based ML pipelines used for accelerator diagnostics (MCP, Ce:YAG, spectrometer images) to identify and classify microinstability signatures in high‑resolution MHD/Vlasov simulation outputs and in synthetic observational diagnostics — and what transfer‑learning or domain‑adaptation steps would be needed to bridge lab/beamline images and simulation data?

Would it be feasible to train physics‑aware surrogate models (PINNs, constrained neural networks, or emulators) to learn closure relations for Braginskii viscosity, suppressed heat flux, or kinetic instability feedback from small‑scale kinetic runs, then embed those surrogates as fast subgrid closures in Arepo / Paicos to accelerate global simulations while retaining conservation and uncertainty estimates?

Can techniques from model‑based optimization in FEL tuning (e.g., undulator taper optimization, sensitivity analyses) inspire ML‑driven adaptive forcing or control strategies in astrophysical simulations — for example to sustain or quench MTI/Kelvin–Helmholtz turbulence — and what are the practical constraints when moving from low‑latency experimental control to batch HPC workflows?

Is there scope for designing joint lab‑simulation validation campaigns where synchrotron/FEL diagnostics are used to create controlled 'analog' measurements (time‑resolved, coherent probes) of collisionless or weakly collisional plasma behavior, enabling direct tests of your synthetic diagnostics and instability closure models?

How could generative ML (normalizing flows, physics‑constrained GANs) be used to produce rare but physically plausible microphysics events (firehose, mirror, whistler bursts) to both augment training sets for detectors/classifiers and to forecast their observable signatures in synthetic X‑ray/synchrotron images — and what physical constraints and metrics would we require to trust those synthetic samples?
12.opening_line: We should explore applying ML techniques from accelerator imaging and control to build physics‑aware surrogates and diagnostics for kinetic plasma instabilities.

11.name: Jonas Berx
discussion_points: GFlowNets for cross-domain sampling: could we test GFlowNet-based samplers to generate ensembles of knotted polymer conformations with prescribed knot type and bending/torsional energy, validate them against Jonas’s BLUES/MCMC samplers, and at the same time try GFlowNets for sampling multi-modal accelerator parameter sets (e.g., undulator taper + bunch compression) to produce diverse Pareto-optimal solutions for FEL performance?

Topological diagnostics for beams: can braid-theory tools (braid group descriptors, Jones polynomial–inspired invariants) that Jonas uses for multichain entanglement be adapted to classify temporal sequences of beamlet/particle trajectories or microbunching maps from Ce:YAG/MCP imaging, to detect coherent instabilities or irreversible mixing in phase space?

Bridging analytic iteration (BLUES) and ML surrogates: would combining Jonas’s BLUES convergence-acceleration schemes with physics-informed ML surrogates reduce the cost of start‑to‑end GENESIS/CSR simulations used for ML training in accelerator optimization (faster data generation for inverse problems and uncertainty quantification)?

Sampling Pareto fronts vs model-based optimization: Francesca’s model-based undulator taper and KMR/GENESIS workflows aim at optimal energy extraction—could GFlowNets or other generative samplers be used to produce diverse, weighted samples of taper schedules that map out Pareto fronts (efficiency vs coherence vs energy spread), and can Jonas’s thermodynamic/Pareto expertise guide objective/regularizer design?

Information–dissipation trade-offs in diagnostics and control: can we quantify the minimal diagnostic information (frame rate, spatial resolution from MCP/Ce:YAG, spectral monitors) required to stabilize a target beam state, using Jonas’s stochastic thermodynamics/Fano-factor bounds together with Francesca’s real diagnostic data and ML inference pipelines to relate information rate to control energy or actuator duty?
11.opening_line: We should explore whether GFlowNets, braid‑theory descriptors and BLUES-style acceleration can be combined to tackle sampling, diagnostics and multi‑objective optimization across knotted polymers and FEL beam physics.

97.name: Christian Bierlich
discussion_points: Could we adapt the normalizing‑flow / HOMER approaches you’ve used for MLHAD to learn and sample full 6D electron‑bunch phase space (including CSR/wakefield‑induced correlations), producing fast, invertible surrogates for start‑to‑end accelerator simulations?

Would a conditional generative model (conditioned on machine settings: gun phase, compression, undulator taper) be viable to emulate expensive GENESIS/GENESIS‑like FEL runs and predict spectra/pulse temporal profiles — and can the uncertainty‑aware reweighting techniques from event‑generator work provide robust error bands when calibrating to measured beamline data?

Can we create a shared, community dataset of synthetic + real accelerator diagnostic images (screens, spectrometers, BPM maps) modeled after MLHAD/Rivet practices, so ML for fault detection, alignment and timing can be trained and validated with reproducible, versioned benchmarks?

Are there useful analogies between string‑level collectivity (string shoving, ropes, junctions) and collective beam phenomena (microbunching, CSR, wakefields) that could inspire new observables or reduced models to detect coherent emission or ‘flow‑like’ signatures in FEL/beamline diagnostics?

How practical is it to build modular, validated ML toolchains for accelerator optimisation by borrowing the PYTHIA/Rivet philosophy—plug‑in physics modules, automated validation tests, and reweightable outputs—to enable end‑to‑end differentiable pipelines for tasks like undulator taper optimisation or bunch‑shaping?
97.opening_line: We should explore combining generative hadronization models with accelerator diagnostics ML to build physics‑aware surrogates.

105.name: Jack Bodine
discussion_points: Segmentation of photon‑source diagnostics: Could we apply Jack’s U‑Net expertise to Ce:YAG/MCP/spectrometer images to automatically extract beam centroid, halo, and coherence proxies — and what labeled image types and ground‑truth metrics (e.g., emittance proxies, FWHM, tail fractions) would be most useful for MAX IV/FLASH diagnostics?

Physics‑aware data augmentation and sim‑to‑real transfer: Francesca, do you have access to GENESIS / start‑to‑end simulation outputs or synthetic diagnostics that we could augment with physically motivated corruptions (scintillator PSF, radiation spikes, CSR‑induced microstructure, camera readnoise, motion blur) to train robust U‑Nets and evaluate domain gap?

Real‑time inference and control‑loop constraints: For deploying segmentation models in feedback (fast BPM/beam‑stabilization), what are the latency, throughput and hardware limits at MAX IV, and would lightweight U‑Net variants, pruning/quantization, or FPGA/GPU edge inference be preferred?

Multimodal fusion and anomaly detection: Could we combine image segmentation outputs with scalar telemetry (bunch charge, cavity phases, BPMs) using contrastive or self‑supervised representations to detect subtle instabilities (timing jitter, microbunching, photocathode degradation) that are hard to label manually?

Training pathway and collaborative project design: Would MAX IV be open to a short pilot project where Jack applies U‑Net segmentation + a curated augmentation suite to a small diagnostics dataset (with Francesca’s mentorship), producing reproducible code, evaluation scripts, and possibly an internship or thesis project bridging accelerator diagnostics and ML?
105.opening_line: We should look at combining U‑Net segmentation with physics‑aware augmentations on MAX IV diagnostics to build a sim‑to‑real pipeline for real‑time beam monitoring.

71.name: Raphael Bonnet Guerrini
discussion_points: Co‑develop interpretable surrogates (e.g., sparse symbolic regression, SHAP‑regularized nets or distilled decision rules) for GENESIS‑level FEL/undulator taper optimization so simulation speedups yield human‑readable control knobs that an operator can trust and validate on the MAX IV linac.

Explore transfer learning between image‑based accelerator diagnostics (Ce:YAG screens, MCPs, beam profile cameras) and pattern recognition used in neutrino/LHC detectors—can pretrained encoders or augmentation strategies reduce label needs and improve robustness across both domains?

Build physics‑informed / Vlasov‑aware ML models (or GP surrogates) for longitudinal phase‑space evolution (bunch compression, CSR, wakefields) that provide calibrated uncertainty and interpretable feature attributions to guide mitigation strategies during machine commissioning.

Design interpretable anomaly‑detection and causal‑attribution pipelines for early detection of component degradation or beam instabilities (spectrometers, BPMs, lasers), with an eye to real‑time deployment constraints and cross‑validation on both accelerator and particle‑physics instrumentation.

Propose a regional collaboration and shared synthetic data bench (federated or simulator‑driven using GENESIS / start‑to‑end sims and detector MC) to benchmark interpretable ML methods across FEL/synchrotron and neutrino/LHC tasks and coordinate validation/transfer protocols.
71.opening_line: We should explore how interpretable ML can connect accelerator diagnostics and particle‑physics reconstruction to enable faster, trustworthy control and discovery.

79.name: Hippolyte Bourel
discussion_points: How could Hippolyte's C‑UCRL equivalence‑aware confidence sets be used to transfer learning across similar accelerator components or operating regimes (e.g., undulator segments, linac sections, or different beam energies), and what would a practical definition of a 'class' C be for accelerator hardware and beam conditions?

Could multi‑stage commissioning and tuning workflows (injector → bunch compression → undulator tapering → diagnostics) be encoded as reward machines to capture non‑Markovian effects like hysteresis, wakefields and long‑term drift, and would that high‑level task structure reduce the number of physical trials required?

What are realistic constraints (shot budget, latency, actuator safety) for on‑line exploration at MAX IV/SXL, and can variance‑aware, time‑uniform concentration and safe‑exploration modifications of UCRL3 provide provable performance while respecting those hardware safety limits?

What is the best way to fuse physics simulators (GENESIS, start‑to‑end Vlasov/CSR models) with model‑based RL — as priors, for offline planning, or for sim‑to‑real fine‑tuning — and how would simulator bias and model mismatch affect regret guarantees and empirical performance?

How can image‑based diagnostics and supervised models for beam state estimation be integrated into a model‑based RL pipeline (state abstraction, clustering, partial observability), and could ApproxEquivalence or clustering discover low‑dimensional regimes where control can be shared across beamlines or operating points?
79.opening_line: We should explore structure‑aware, variance‑sensitive model‑based RL to speed and safely automate FEL/linac tuning using diagnostics and simulations.

115.name: Jan-Matthias Braun
discussion_points: Explore implementing physics‑informed, low‑latency neural networks on FPGA/embedded hardware for real‑time FEL/accelerator feedback (targets: timing jitter, microbunching/CSR onset, pulse energy fluctuations) — leveraging Jan‑Matthias's efficient LSTM/echo‑state FPGA toolchains and Francesca's diagnostic streams.

Combine nonlinear/chaos analysis (Lyapunov spectra, recurrence quantification) with data‑driven models to identify early precursors of beam instabilities and microbunching; test whether chaos‑aware features improve prediction horizons versus pure ML or kinetic models alone.

Develop a simulation→experiment transfer pipeline: train on GENESIS / start‑to‑end simulations and adapt to Ce:YAG, MCP and spectrometer images using domain adaptation, physics‑aware losses and calibrated uncertainty estimates so operators can trust automated corrective actions.

Translate explainable anomaly‑detection and autoencoder graph methods from biomedical imaging to accelerator diagnostics: apply lightweight explainable models to camera and BPM images for component health monitoring, and co‑design visualization/interpretation tools for beamline engineers.

Co‑design new fast diagnostics (sensor + embedded ML) for on‑the‑fly undulator taper optimization and bunch shaping — e.g., compressed imaging or photodiode arrays feeding FPGA reservoir computers to shorten the loop between measurement, model prediction, and actuator commands.
115.opening_line: We should explore deploying physics‑informed, low‑latency ML on edge hardware to predict and mitigate nonlinear beam instabilities in FELs.

69.name: Nuno Brás
discussion_points: Can we build a physics‑informed diffusion model that jointly incorporates optical forward models from corneal light scattering and synchrotron/beamline optics (e.g., point‑spread functions, scattering kernels) to do denoising and super‑resolution for both OCT/corneal images and Ce:YAG/streak/screen images—using a U‑Net as the score/denoiser and embedding the forward operator into the loss?

How transferable are U‑Net segmentation strategies developed for corneal layer delineation to accelerator imaging tasks (beam‑spot segmentation, scintillator artefact removal, component damage detection)? Let’s discuss concrete domain‑adaptation plans (sim2real, self‑supervision, few‑shot fine‑tuning) and minimum labelled datasets needed for robust performance.

Could we use GANs or conditioned diffusion models to generate realistic rare events (beam loss patterns, CSR microbunching signatures, or pathological corneal scattering) constrained by conservation laws and accelerator physics (energy/momentum) to improve anomaly detection and uncertainty calibration?

What interpretability and uncertainty‑quantification techniques are most meaningful for clinicians and operators respectively? For example, would counterfactual explanations, concept activation vectors tied to physical parameters (scattering coefficient, emittance), or calibrated predictive intervals help with trust and real‑time decision making in both the clinic and the control room?

Given Francesca’s interest in Oresund ML collaborations and Nuno’s translational/entrepreneurship background, can we design a pilot regional program: shared datasets/instrument time (MAX IV optics diagnostics + ophthalmic images), joint PhD/postdoc placements, and a roadmap for technology transfer—what funding calls and data‑governance models should we target?
69.opening_line: We should explore physics‑aware generative and segmentation tools that translate between corneal optics and accelerator imaging.

27.name: Pietro Butti
discussion_points: Use autoencoders + conditional normalizing flows on Ce:YAG/MCP and other beamline images to learn a compact latent space correlated with physical beam parameters (energy spread, emittance, timing jitter); evaluate whether the latent coordinates can be used for rapid inverse tuning (predict actuator changes) and anomaly detection during operations.

Develop neural‑ODE / stochastic neural‑ODE surrogates for longitudinal phase‑space evolution that include CSR and wakefield stochasticity, trained on high‑fidelity start‑to‑end simulations (e.g., GENESIS) and limited measurement data, with the goal of achieving 10–100× faster prediction for online control or uncertainty quantification.

Adapt normalizing‑flow and Monte‑Carlo acceleration techniques from lattice QFT to accelerate sampling of high‑dimensional particle distributions and rare events in accelerator simulations (halo and loss tails); benchmark flows against importance sampling and existing particle‑tracking Monte Carlo for accuracy and compute cost.

Apply renormalization/grouping ideas from lattice/epidemic percolation work to build multiscale coarse‑grained models of collective instabilities (microbunching, beam breakup): use ML to discover effective degrees of freedom at different scales and test whether RG‑style scaling laws predict instability onset across beamline sections.

Create physics‑informed generative datasets (using Pietro’s experience with nonperturbative regimes) to synthesize rare/failure modes in accelerator components for supervised ML training — e.g., realistic, labeled microbunching or cavity‑breakdown scenarios — and run cross‑validation on real diagnostic streams to close the sim‑to‑real gap.
27.opening_line: We should explore whether lattice‑inspired normalizing flows and neural‑ODE surrogates can both compress FEL start‑to‑end physics and sharpen beamline diagnostics.

96.name: William Bærenholdt
discussion_points: Compare extreme‑value and tail‑risk techniques from actuarial science (POT, EVT, compound‑Poisson frameworks) with anomaly detection for rare beam instabilities — can EVT improve detection thresholds, false‑alarm control and capital/stability buffer design?

Adapt physics‑informed ML used in FEL and beam dynamics (explicit conservation laws, wakefield/CSR models, dispersion constraints) as inductive priors for actuarial ML to enforce monotonicity, reserving/pricing constraints and improve interpretability for regulators.

Explore sim‑to‑real and domain‑adaptation workflows: use start‑to‑end accelerator simulators (GENESIS, Vlasov/Kinetic solvers) to synthesize labeled anomalous images/signals for robust detectors — could similar synthetic augmentation address scarce labeled insurance claim images or rare catastrophic claim scenarios?

Jointly develop uncertainty‑quantification and stress‑testing pipelines: compare Bayesian/ensemble/evidential UQ used in capital models with sensitivity studies in accelerator physics (CSR, wakefields, jitter), and design shared metrics that map ML uncertainty to operational decisions and regulatory stress tests.

Concrete master‑thesis bridges: e.g., model claims arrivals and beam loss/instability events as temporal point processes with covariates; build fast interpretable surrogates of GENESIS for real‑time control and capital estimation; or transfer self‑supervised representations between accelerator images and insurance imagery for anomaly/fraud detection.
96.opening_line: We should explore where actuarial tail‑risk modelling and accelerator diagnostics' ML can learn from each other.

112.name: Sascha Caron
discussion_points: Can we adapt Sascha's deep generative pipelines (VAEs/GANs with a density‑information buffer and frequency correction) to create ultra‑fast, high‑fidelity start‑to‑end surrogates for FEL/linac simulations (e.g., replace parts of GENESIS or CSR/CSR wakefield propagation) so that we can generate realistic Ce:YAG/BPM/spectrometer image stacks orders of magnitude faster for design and ML training?

How would a DeepXS‑style surrogate for expensive physics outputs (NLO cross‑sections analogue) perform for tasks Francesca cares about—e.g., predicting gain curves, optimum undulator taper profiles or EEHG sensitivity measures—and what approaches would we need to quantify and propagate the surrogate uncertainty back into taper optimization and control loops?

Could we port the anomaly‑detection toolset developed for collider searches (ensemble One‑Class DSVD + normalizing flows, mixture‑of‑theories training, DDD) to online beam diagnostics to detect subtle, nonstationary faults (CSR blow‑up, timing jitter, photocathode degradation) in image and scalar streams, and what training regime (sim/real mix, domain adaptation) would make it robust in the noisy accelerator environment?

There is shared interest in low‑latency inference: shall we design a small hardware+software prototype (neuromorphic/FPGA/edge GPU) that runs transformer/graph tracking or lightweight generative models on accelerator diagnostics for real‑time feedback (bunch arrival time, centroid drift), and benchmark energy/latency like Sascha's neuromorphic studies at MAX IV testbeds?

Would it be worthwhile to launch a joint, open benchmark (an 'Accelerator Machines' challenge) — curated simulated + experimental datasets (Ce:YAG/BPM images, spectra, timing traces) with standardized metrics for fidelity, uncertainty calibration, and anomaly detection — to drive reproducible ML tools and enable direct transfer of LHC‑style model‑recasting and profile‑likelihood inference into accelerator commissioning and FEL optimization?
112.opening_line: We should explore applying uncertainty‑aware, high‑speed ML surrogates and anomaly detectors from collider physics to accelerate and stabilize FEL/beam diagnostics and optimization.
