26.name: Jerome Chenevez
discussion_points: Transfer learning for rare events: could models trained on astrophysical burst catalogs (e.g., MINBAR time series, FITS‑stored lightcurves) be adapted to detect rare beam instabilities or vacuum/gun events in accelerator diagnostics, and conversely could high‑fidelity accelerator simulations (GENESIS, start‑to‑end) be used to augment training for uncommon astrophysical transients?

Low‑latency pipelines and hardware: both our fields need sub‑ms timing and immediate reaction (burst follow‑up, beam feedback). Can we compare timing and data‑acquisition stacks (NICER/INTEGRAL time‑tagging, INTEGRAL mosaicking vs. MAX IV timing/overlap systems, Ce:YAG/MCP monitors) and co‑design GPU/FPGA ML inference for on‑device transient detection and closed‑loop control?

Image and graph representations of instrumentation: mosaicked X‑ray detector images and component images from accelerator diagnostics are structurally similar—would graph neural networks that encode instrument geometry (detector adjacency, beamline element connectivity) improve source localization, calibration, or fault diagnosis across both domains?

Physics‑informed spectral/temporal ML: we both extract spectral signatures (cyclotron lines, reflection spectra; FEL coherence, harmonic content). Could we jointly develop ML models that enforce physical constraints (conservation laws, phase‑space structure) to improve interpretability and robust uncertainty quantification for line fitting, QPO detection and FEL spectral characterization?

Shared benchmark dataset and collaboration seed: would creating a curated cross‑domain benchmark (FITS images/time series from X‑ray missions + labeled accelerator images/time series and simulated ground truth) hosted for Øresund ML groups accelerate collaborations, allow standardized anomaly/ transient metrics, and attract ML students to co‑develop methods?
26.opening_line: We should explore building shared ML pipelines to detect and characterize fast transients and diagnostics signals across X‑ray astronomy and accelerator instrumentation.

87.name: Clément Cherblamc
discussion_points: Adaptation of super‑resolution U‑Net pipelines to accelerator diagnostics: discuss applying Clément’s climate super‑resolution architectures to Ce:YAG, MCP and spectrometer images to recover finer beam structure (transverse profiles, microbunching signatures) and link the recovered features to FEL performance metrics like coherence and spectral purity; what ground‑truth or high‑resolution simulations exist for supervised training and what SNR/artefact statistics must the models handle?

Synthetic data, sim‑to‑real transfer and domain adaptation: combine Francesca’s start‑to‑end GENESIS/beamline simulations and diagnostics models with climate‑style data generation to create realistic training sets for ML on rare or hard‑to‑measure accelerator states (and conversely use accelerator simulation‑to‑real techniques to improve synthetic polar climate fields used for downscaling); what simulator outputs, metadata and noise models would be needed to make transfer learning feasible?

Physics‑aware surrogate models across PDE systems: both polar ice dynamics (surface mass balance, SMB) and beam dynamics (Vlasov/CSR effects) are governed by conservation laws—compare opportunities for PINNs or hybrid physics+U‑Net surrogates to speed up parameter studies, provide uncertainty estimates, and enforce physical constraints; which conserved quantities and boundary/initial conditions are essential in each domain and what are acceptable computational budgets for surrogate evaluation?

Temporal resolution, timing diagnostics and reconstruction methods: explore cross‑fertilization between ultrafast timing/reconstruction techniques used for FELs (RF deflectors, streaking, phase‑jump diagnostics) and climate time‑series super/temporal‑resolution or deconvolution approaches—could ML methods for reconstructing femtosecond‑scale beam profiles inspire new ways to reconstruct high‑frequency signals in remote sensing of polar processes, or vice versa?

Uncertainty/sensitivity frameworks and model‑based optimization: Francesca’s model‑based undulator taper optimization and sensitivity/mitigation studies could be paralleled with climate parameter sensitivity and data‑assimilation approaches—discuss building shared benchmarks for uncertainty‑aware ML, criteria for accepting ML‑driven control/parameter estimates in operational settings, and a pilot project (e.g., optimizing an imaging pipeline or a local SMB emulator) to compare methods.
87.opening_line: We should explore how U‑net super‑resolution, sim‑to‑real and physics‑aware surrogates can link beam diagnostics and polar climate modeling.

31.name: Daniel Lomholt Christensen
discussion_points: How would we construct a graph representation of a full instrument chain—whether a neutron guide plus sample environment or an accelerator beamline with diagnostics—so that nodes/edges encode the right physics (optical elements, scattering centers, mechanical degrees of freedom, detector noise) for GNN‑based inverse design and fault diagnosis?

Could we turn McStas/GENESIS start‑to‑end pipelines into differentiable or fast surrogate models (physics‑informed NNs, normalizing flows, or GNN surrogates) to enable amortized inference of 'what made the dataset'—i.e., infer instrument configuration or sample/environment parameters from measurements?

What are the key differences and commonalities in detector and camera image statistics (neutron position‑sensitive detectors vs MCP/Ce:YAG/CCD beamline images), and can we build physics‑aware denoising, domain‑adaptation, or anomaly‑detection models that transfer across those sensor types if we incorporate sensor noise models explicitly?

Could enforcing physics constraints in graph architectures (phase‑space conservation, flux/energy balance, symmetries) help with interpretable, uncertainty‑aware optimization of engineering tradeoffs—e.g., piecewise linear neutron guides versus manufactured elliptical guides, or undulator taper profiles for FELs?

What would a minimal collaborative benchmark look like for the Oresund region: a small suite of simulated + measured examples (neutron transport through a guide; beam profiles from linac/BPMs) to test GNN surrogates, sim‑to‑real transfer strategies, and causal/inverse‑modeling approaches—what metrics and shared tooling should we prioritize?
31.opening_line: We should explore encoding beamlines and sample environments as graphs to enable inverse, physics‑aware ML across neutron and photon instruments.

49.name: Hans Christiansen
discussion_points: Sim-to-real transfer: compare challenges in moving from high-fidelity beamline/accelerator simulations to real diagnostics (images, monitors) with Hans's simulated data for strongly correlated systems—could we co-develop physics-aware domain adaptation (cycleGAN/physics-constrained flows, domain-adversarial training) and a joint benchmark to quantify sim-to-real gaps?

Surrogate/emulator strategies for costly forward models: exchange approaches for building fast ML emulators of GENESIS/beam-dynamics and of many‑body solvers (DMRG/DMFT/QMC), including uncertainty quantification (deep ensembles, Bayesian NNs) and active learning for targeted parameter scans to reduce expensive simulations on both sides.

Real‑time tuning and control: explore adapting RL/optimal-control approaches used for online accelerator tuning (beam steering, bunch compression) to laboratory control problems in quantum-transport experiments (gate voltages, temperature, drive pulses) and conversely bring precision control ideas from condensed-matter to improve automated beamline stabilization.

Coherence and spectral diagnostics as a shared language: discuss methods Francesca uses to characterize temporal/spectral coherence in FEL pulses (phase retrieval, coherence metrics) and whether analogous signal-processing/ML tools could reveal emergent coherence or subtle spectral signatures of new phases in transport and spectroscopic data (ARPES, optical conductivity).

Imaging and end-to-end pipelines: identify a concrete pilot—use MAX IV imaging/ptychography or soft X‑ray beamlines to probe candidate correlated materials and co-design ML pipelines (denoising, reconstruction, anomaly/phase classification) leveraging Francesca's diagnostics data formats and Hans's physics priors to accelerate discovery.
49.opening_line: Let's explore how our simulation-driven ML for beam diagnostics and many‑body materials can cross‑pollinate to speed discovery, control, and coherence detection.

95.name: Daniel Alejandro Daza Valdebenito
discussion_points: Compare how autoencoders (bottleneck compression, denoising, latent-space anomaly detection) could be applied to both Ce:YAG / MCP / spectrometer images from accelerators and multi-epoch protostellar images — what architecture choices, loss functions (e.g., perceptual vs. physics-conserving), and latent-space interpretability would be most useful for preserving physics (flux, PSF, coherence)?

Exchange strategies for sim-to-real / domain adaptation: both of you rely heavily on simulations (GENESIS / start‑to‑end for FELs; radiative transfer / MCRT for disks). Discuss concrete approaches — cycleGAN, domain-adaptive fine-tuning, physics-informed losses or calibrated forward models — and propose a benchmark task (synthetic→real) to evaluate transfer methods across the two domains.

Explore Siamese / contrastive networks for cross-epoch matching and morphological similarity: Daniel could use them to link features across observations (e.g., moving clumps, rings, gaps), while Francesca could use the same idea to detect subtle changes in beam profiles or align diagnostics across detectors — talk about suitable data augmentations, distance metrics, and evaluation criteria for low-SNR, high-dynamic-range images.

Discuss uncertainty quantification and interpretability requirements for scientific deployment: compare methods (ensembles, Bayesian NNs, evidential deep learning, calibrated predictors) and how to present uncertainties to instrument/control systems (real-time beam tuning vs. cataloguing protostellar substructures), and whether disentangled/physically-structured latent spaces could map to meaningful parameters (grain size, eccentricity, emittance, energy spread).

Propose small, concrete collaborative projects leveraging regional resources: e.g., build a shared synthetic/real paired dataset and run a 2‑day hackathon to adapt an autoencoder pipeline for both datasets; organize short lab visits to swap knowledge about high-frame-rate detectors, timing jitter mitigation, and pre-processing pipelines; or co-develop a surrogate model to replace expensive forward sims for faster inference in both accelerator and disk modelling.
95.opening_line: We should compare autoencoder and sim‑to‑real strategies used for accelerator diagnostics and protostellar imaging to find common ML building blocks.

55.name: Diana Vigah Adetsu
discussion_points: Uncertainty-aware deep learning: explore how Diana's interest in Bayesian Neural Networks and probabilistic kriging could be combined with Daniel's planned DNN/autoencoder pipelines to produce calibrated uncertainties for inverse problems (peat thickness mapping vs. disk structure inference).

Sensor-hierarchies ↔ multi-wavelength strategies: map Diana's sensor-hierarchy and on-the-go survey workflows (drone GR, EMI, GPR, LiDAR) to observational scheduling for protostellar studies (ALMA, JWST, submm), and discuss algorithmic rules to prioritize instruments under limited observing time.

Domain-specific forward models + ML: compare how physics-based forward modeling (EM responses of peat layers vs. radiative transfer in protoplanetary disks) can be used to generate synthetic training data, regularize DNNs/autoencoders, and validate inversion outputs across both fields.

Sampling, active learning and sparse labels: adapt optimal sampling and validation strategies from geophysical field campaigns (sample-size assessments, spatial cross-validation) to astronomical observation planning and active selection of protostar targets for efficient DNN training.

Representation learning and similarity metrics: investigate using autoencoders and Siamese networks to learn compact latent spaces for (a) geophysical signatures of peatland types and (b) multi-epoch/multi-wavelength protostar observations, enabling anomaly detection, transfer learning, or cross-domain methodological benchmarks.
55.opening_line: We should compare how multi-instrument data, physics-based simulations, and uncertainty-aware neural nets can address sparse, noisy inverse problems in our respective domains.

18.name: Noah Al-Khulaifi
discussion_points: Sub‑pixel localization and PSF deconvolution: compare single‑molecule localization pipelines (e.g., DeepSTORM/ThunderSTORM, Gaussian fitting) with star/feature centroiding and deconvolution in protostellar images — could microscopy localization networks be adapted to find disk substructures or vice versa?

Denoising and autoencoders for faint-signal extraction: explore using denoising/variational autoencoders (or physics‑informed VAEs) to recover faint binding events in nanowire signals and faint disk substructures in noisy multi-epoch observations, including how to encode instrument noise models (shot noise, read noise, electrical noise) into the training process.

Siamese and few‑shot approaches for matching rare events across epochs/sensors: discuss applying Siamese networks or metric‑learning methods to match single binding signatures across devices or to match protostellar/disk features across observations with different PSFs and wavelengths, and how to leverage synthetic examples for few‑shot calibration.

Simulation-driven training and differentiable forward models: compare the feasibility of building differentiable simulators (nanowire electrical/optical response vs. radiative transfer + telescope optics like RADMC-3D) to generate labeled training data and perform domain randomization — could we share noise/forward‑modeling toolkits or jointly develop modular simulators?

Physical interpretability and uncertainty quantification: share strategies for producing scientifically meaningful outputs (binding kinetics, particle counts, dust mass, gap depths) with calibrated uncertainties — discuss Bayesian DNNs, ensembles, posterior‑aware loss functions, and hybrid ML+physics inversion schemes to prevent physically implausible reconstructions.
18.opening_line: We should compare how sub‑pixel localization and denoising challenges in our instruments map onto each other's datasets.

36.name: Dmitry Baranov
discussion_points: Can we adapt sequence models and transformers used for time‑resolved spectroscopy to invert sparse Fourier/visibility data from interferometers (e.g., ALMA) — treating visibilities as sequences and using Dmitry’s multilayer‑diffraction expertise to build physics‑informed priors for image reconstruction?

How could autoencoders and Siamese networks be used for sensitive change detection across epochs in both domains — for example, detecting subtle spectral shifts or aging signatures in perovskites and small morphological changes or emerging substructures in multi‑epoch protoplanetary disk images?

Would a graph representation and graph neural networks provide a common language for mesoscale assembly: map nanocrystal superlattices (nodes = particles/platelets, edges = binding/spacing) and dust/pebble aggregates in disks to the same modeling framework to predict emergent optical/scattering signatures from local interaction rules?

Could we build conditional generative models (VAEs/diffusion models or physics‑conditioned GANs) trained on forward simulators (DFT + scattering for perovskites; radiative‑transfer and dust‑growth models for disks) to produce realistic labeled datasets and then study domain adaptation/transfer learning between lab and astro synthetic data?

Is there scope to share active‑learning and experiment/observation‑design strategies — e.g., uncertainty‑aware ML that recommends the next pump‑probe delay or the next interferometric baseline/wavelength to observe — leveraging Dmitry’s lab automation experience and Daniel’s telescope scheduling constraints?
36.opening_line: We should explore how generative and representation‑learning techniques could reconstruct structures from sparse diffraction and interferometric data.

12.name: Thomas Berlok
discussion_points: Could we train convolutional or variational autoencoders on high‑resolution MHD/Vlasov outputs to compress microscale instability signatures into a latent space, then regress from that latent space to effective subgrid transport coefficients (e.g., Braginskii viscosity, suppressed conductivity) for use in large‑scale Arepo runs?

How feasible is a Siamese‑network pipeline that learns a distance metric between multiwavelength protostellar images and synthetic diagnostics from our simulations, so we can quantify degeneracies between dust physics, magnetic topology, and viewing geometry when performing parameter inference?

Can we develop ML‑based surrogate closures for mirror/firehose/whistler feedback (trained on targeted kinetic simulations) that enforce conservation and stability constraints and are deployable as modular subroutines in Psecas/Paicos/Arepo—what validation and uncertainty quantification would be required?

Would unsupervised autoencoder/anomaly‑detection applied to time series of simulation fields be a useful way to flag rare instability onsets or magnetic amplification events, and then automatically generate synthetic observables to propose observational signatures for Daza's protostellar data?

What practical HPC and reproducibility workflow should we adopt to bridge our groups—data formats, I/O for large Arepo/Vlasov dumps, GPU training resources at NBI, versioned training sets and notebooks—so a newcomer to DNNs can reproduce results and we can publish ML‑ready benchmark datasets?
12.opening_line: Let's identify ML strategies that connect our high‑resolution plasma simulations with multiwavelength protostellar observations.

11.name: Jonas Berx
discussion_points: GFlowNets + topology: explore training a GFlowNet conditioned on topological invariants (e.g., knot type or Jones/Alexander polynomial) to generate diverse knotted polymer conformations, and discuss how Daniel could help implement/scale the deep-network components while Jonas provides the topological/physical constraints and evaluation metrics.

Autoencoder latent spaces as shared coordinates: use convolutional or graph autoencoders to compress high-dimensional polymer conformation ensembles and protostellar disk images/simulations into low-dimensional latent representations, then compare whether topological transitions in polymers map to morphological transitions in disks — this could reveal transferable architectures and loss terms that preserve topology-sensitive features.

Siamese networks for morphology matching: build Siamese networks to measure similarity between observed disk substructures and simulated outputs (or between different knotted conformations) to perform model selection and rapid matching; discuss datasets, augmentation strategies, and what physically meaningful distance metrics (braid descriptors, persistence homology) should be paired with the learned embedding.

Predicting topological invariants from data: investigate whether DNNs can be trained to predict knot-theoretic invariants (Jones polynomial coefficients, braid signatures) directly from 3D coordinates or 2D projections, and conversely whether networks trained on astrophysical images can learn compact topological descriptors of spiral/filament entanglement — this bridges Jonas's braid-theory tools and Daniel's imaging data.

Speeding forward models for ML training via BLUES and analytic acceleration: discuss adapting Jonas's BLUES/iteration-acceleration methods to accelerate PDE/ODE solvers used in protoplanetary-disk simulations (e.g., simplified hydrodynamics or radiative-transfer surrogates), enabling generation of large labeled datasets for Daniel's DNNs and for training generative samplers of rare topological states.
11.opening_line: We should explore using generative ML and topology-aware embeddings to connect knotted polymer sampling with protostellar-disk morphology analysis.

97.name: Christian Bierlich
discussion_points: Conditional generative models (normalizing flows, HOMER-like architectures) for fast, multi-wavelength protostar/disk observation emulators: what would it take to condition on physical parameters (mass, accretion rate, grain-size distribution) and export calibrated uncertainties like HEP event generators do?

Combine autoencoders and Siamese networks to build a simulation-informed similarity metric and unsupervised catalog of disk substructures — could HEP practices for anomaly detection and event-level feature engineering translate to robust, low-label discovery in protostellar images?

Uncertainty-aware reweighting and automated theory variations (Christian's fragmentation/reweighting tools): can we reweight existing radiative-transfer / hydrodynamic simulation outputs to explore dust physics parameter space without re-running expensive sims, and how would that integrate with training DNNs?

Physics‑informed architectures and interaction models: both hadronization collectivity and dust coagulation are emergent many-body phenomena — might graph/particle‑based neural networks or explicit interaction modules (inspired by string models) provide better inductive biases than generic CNNs for both domains?

Reproducible, community datasets and validation pipelines: could we design an open benchmark (simulations + real observations + standardized metrics) for protostar ML similar to MLHAD/Rivet, leveraging Christian's experience in public tooling to accelerate Daniel's early-PhD workflows and future cross-field comparisons?
97.opening_line: We should explore adapting HEP generative emulators and reweighting pipelines to accelerate protostellar disk inference.

105.name: Jack Bodine
discussion_points: Segmentation of disk substructures with U‑Nets: what specific labels (rings, gaps, spirals, clumps, shadows) and ground truth sources (hand labels, synthetic RADMC‑3D/MCFOST images, CLEANed ALMA products) do we each have or can create, and how should we design augmentations that preserve physically important quantities (total flux, beam shape, spectral index)?

Autoencoders as physics‑aware priors and denoisers: could we use a VAE/denoising autoencoder trained on synthetic and observed protostar+dust images to (a) compress multi‑wavelength observations into a latent space for downstream tasks, (b) reconstruct missing bands, and (c) flag anomalous substructures that deviate from model priors?

Siamese / contrastive networks to link features across epochs and wavelengths: how feasible is it to train a Siamese network that learns invariance to PSF/beam convolution and noise, so we can robustly match and track the same dust features (e.g., vortices, clumps) in multi‑epoch ALMA or scattered‑light datasets?

Physics‑guided augmentation and sim‑to‑real transfer: drawing on Jack’s IEC fusion diagnostics experience with sensor artifacts, can we design realistic augmentation pipelines (beam convolution, correlated noise, pointing errors, radiative‑transfer parameter sweeps) and domain adaptation strategies (feature alignment, CycleGAN with physics constraints) to close the gap between hydro/radiative simulations and real telescope images?

A concrete pilot pipeline and evaluation plan: would a collaborative prototype that goes from hydrodynamic+radiative simulations -> controlled augmentations -> U‑Net segmentation + autoencoder latent regularizer -> Siamese temporal association, validated on a small ALMA protostar sample, be a good first joint project — and what compute, labeled data, and astrophysical tests (e.g., comparing inferred gap depths to synthetic opacities) would we need?
105.opening_line: We should explore how U‑Net segmentation, autoencoded priors, and Siamese matching can together reveal and track dust substructures in multi‑epoch protostar observations.

71.name: Raphael Bonnet Guerrini
discussion_points: Interpretable latent spaces for autoencoders: discuss architectures (β‑VAE, disentangled VAEs, conditional VAEs) and interpretability tools (TCAV, concept vectors, mutual information probing) to map latent dimensions to concrete dust/ disk physical parameters (grain size distribution, surface density, gap radius) and how to validate those mappings with synthetic radiative‑transfer models.

Siamese and contrastive networks for multi-epoch / multi-wavelength matching: explore using Siamese or contrastive embeddings to match protostellar observations across instruments/epochs (handling PSF/beam differences) and compare that to similarity learning used in LHC/neutrino event classification—what loss functions, augmentation strategies, and interpretability checks work best?

Unsupervised anomaly detection across domains: examine adapting unsupervised anomaly-detection pipelines from transient/neutrino searches (autoencoders, normalizing flows, deep one‑class) to find unusual substructures or variability in protoplanetary disks; propose injection/recovery tests with RADMC‑3D or MHD simulations to quantify sensitivity and failure modes.

Physics‑aware training and calibrated uncertainties: how to incorporate forward radiative‑transfer or simple physics constraints (differentiable surrogates, physics‑informed losses) and use likelihood‑free inference / deep ensembles / conformal methods from particle physics to produce physically meaningful, well‑calibrated posteriors on dust parameters inferred by DNNs.

Shared synthetic-data benchmarks and interpretability audits: propose creating cross‑domain simulated datasets (detector‑style noise for neutrino/LHC and synthetic disk images) plus interpretability benchmark tasks to study how simulation priors bias learned features and to enable transfer learning or domain adaptation between particle and astrophysical pipelines.
71.opening_line: We should explore how interpretable DNNs and autoencoders can link latent features to physical dust properties and rare transient signatures.

79.name: Hippolyte Bourel
discussion_points: Use autoencoders or Siamese nets to learn compact, instrument-agnostic embeddings of multi-wavelength protostar observations, then treat those embeddings as states for Hippolyte-style model-based RL or bandits — how would we define state equivalence and exploit ApproxEquivalence/C-UCRL to aggregate similar protostellar states and reduce sample complexity?

Frame telescope scheduling / exposure-control for protostar monitoring as an average-reward MDP or nonstationary bandit: what concrete reward should we optimize (information gain, SNR, detection of substructures, or long-term tracking of dust evolution), and how could variance-aware UCRL3-style confidence sets minimize regret across an extended observing campaign?

Encode scientific goals that are intrinsically temporal (e.g., confirm formation of a gap, observe a transient accretion event) as reward machines or temporal-logic tasks so RL can exploit high-level structure — what domain-specific predicates (spectral index thresholds, spatial asymmetry metrics) would map to automaton states?

Merge uncertainty estimates from DNNs (calibrated predictive distributions, ensemble or dropout-based estimates) with Hippolyte's time-uniform/variance-aware concentration bounds to drive principled exploration: how do we calibrate neural uncertainty so it can enter confidence sets and yield meaningful regret guarantees in practice?

Build physics-informed simulators / synthetic catalogs of protoplanetary disks to jointly train autoencoders and model-based planners, then study transfer to real observations; could clustering of simulated+real data reveal equivalence classes (C in C-UCRL) that speed up real-world learning, and how do we handle the sim-to-real gap?
79.opening_line: We should combine autoencoder-based embeddings with model-based RL to adaptively schedule and optimize protostar observations.

115.name: Jan-Matthias Braun
discussion_points: Compare purely data-driven autoencoders with physics‑informed autoencoders that enforce mass/angular momentum conservation and dust coagulation/fragmentation rules — test on synthetic hydrodynamic + dust-evolution simulations and multiwavelength observations to see which latent features correspond to physically meaningful disk substructures.

Adapt Siamese-network architectures to quantify morphological similarity of rings, gaps, and spirals across wavelengths and epochs, then use explainability techniques from biomedical imaging to map which physical observables (e.g., optical depth, grain size indicators) drive the network's similarity judgments.

Evaluate hardware‑friendly recurrent/reservoir designs (novel LSTM nodes, echo‑state networks, FPGA implementations) for time-series tasks in protostellar variability and episodic accretion: benchmark forecast skill, latency, and power consumption to determine feasibility for on‑telescope or small‑sat edge inference.

Bring chaos and nonlinear-systems diagnostics (embedding dimension, Lyapunov spectra) into the analysis pipeline for disk instabilities and dust evolution, and combine those diagnostics with reservoir computing to both classify dynamical regimes and produce short-term trajectory forecasts of observables.

Co-design an explainable anomaly-detection pipeline: energy‑efficient autoencoder compression + interpretable latent-space triggers for rare substructures or transient events, validated end-to-end from simulated data to lab hardware — leveraging Jan‑Matthias's embedded/HLS toolchains and Daniel's observing plans for protostars.
115.opening_line: We should explore physics‑informed autoencoders and low‑power hardware to reveal the nonlinear dynamics shaping protoplanetary dust substructures.

69.name: Nuno Brás
discussion_points: How could diffusion-based denoising and super-resolution pipelines you’ve applied to corneal OCT be adapted to improve signal-to-noise and recover faint substructures in protostellar disk images, once we account for astronomical PSFs and radiative-transfer noise characteristics?

Can we treat corneal light-scattering and dust-grain scattering as related inverse problems—are there transferable parameterizations or physics-informed constraints (e.g., on phase functions or size distributions) that let a single ML framework infer scatterer properties across both domains?

Given Daniel’s interest in autoencoders and Siamese nets and Nuno’s work on interpretability, could we build latent-space diagnostics or metric-learning schemes that map learned embeddings to physical quantities (optical depth, grain size, transparency index) and quantify epistemic/aleatoric uncertainty for those estimates?

What is the best way to generate and validate synthetic training data for rare or evolving morphologies—could GANs or conditional diffusion models produce physically plausible disk substructures or corneal pathologies, and how would we incorporate forward physics (radiative transfer or scattering simulators) to ensure realism?

Might a multi-scale, physics-informed U-Net architecture (anisotropic kernels, scattering-aware loss, PSF-deconvolution blocks) serve both corneal-layer segmentation and hierarchical disk-substructure detection, and what task-specific modifications (labeling strategy, temporal/Siamese modules) would each domain require?
69.opening_line: We should explore physics-informed generative and segmentation models that link light-scattering problems in corneas and protoplanetary disks.

27.name: Pietro Butti
discussion_points: Can we train autoencoders on Monte‑Carlo–generated radiative‑transfer images (using Pietro's experience generating controlled synthetic ensembles) to learn a compact latent space that reliably separates dust grain size/opacity effects from geometric substructures seen in Daniel's multi‑wavelength protostar observations?

Could we model the temporal evolution of disk substructures (spiral arms, rings, clumps, accretion bursts) in that latent space using Neural ODEs / Stochastic Neural ODEs, combining Pietro's work on latent dynamics for non‑equilibrium systems with Daniel's planned time‑series or multi‑epoch imaging — what cadence and noise levels would make this feasible?

Would normalizing flows be a practical route for likelihood‑free inference of dust and disk parameters, where Pietro supplies large Monte‑Carlo forward models for training and Daniel provides observational priors (wavelength coverage, PSF, calibration)? What observables (SED + resolved images) should we prioritize to break degeneracies in grain size distributions?

How about using Siamese or contrastive networks to learn a similarity metric between simulation outputs and real disk images so we can do domain adaptation/weak supervision — e.g., label a few high‑confidence morphologies and let the network find matching structures in noisy surveys; how many labeled examples could Daniel realistically provide?

Let's explore RG‑inspired coarse‑graining and percolation analogies to characterize multiscale disk phenomena (dust growth, gap opening, pebble traps): can concepts from Pietro's work on scale separation in field theory reveal critical scales or universality in disk substructure formation that we can test against observational statistics?
27.opening_line: We could combine physics‑informed Monte‑Carlo simulations and latent‑space dynamics to better interpret multi‑wavelength protostellar disk observations.

96.name: William Bærenholdt
discussion_points: Both our domains deal with rare, heavy-tailed events—can we compare approaches for tail modelling and uncertainty calibration (extreme-value theory, heavy-tailed losses, Bayesian/ensemble uncertainty in DNNs) to improve prediction and risk quantification for insurance claims and protostellar outbursts or episodic accretion events?

Autoencoders are central to Daniel's interests and can also serve as unsupervised detectors in claims data—shall we prototype a shared pipeline (denoising/VAE + reconstruction score) to compress multi-wavelength protostar observations and to flag anomalous claim patterns, then compare how reconstruction-loss thresholds map to physical anomalies vs fraudulent/atypical claims?

Siamese and metric-learning ideas could help with record linkage and matching: could we adapt a Siamese network trained to identify whether two observations are the same protostar (across instruments/epochs) to the actuarial problem of linking duplicate or related claims, and what invariances (rotation/flux scaling vs claim metadata shifts) are needed?

Actuarial credibility and hierarchical shrinkage are powerful for small-data regimes—how could we use credibility priors or Bayesian hierarchical layers to regularize DNNs when protostar samples are few, and conversely can deep representations or transfer learning improve reserving/forecasting in sub-portfolios with limited claims?

We both rely on simulations—should we compare sim-to-real strategies: using physically simulated protoplanetary disk images for pretraining and domain adaptation for real telescope data, alongside synthetic claim generation or adversarial augmentation for rare-event training; and discuss how interpretability (feature attributions, physics constraints) affects acceptance in scientific vs regulatory settings?
96.opening_line: We should explore parallels between modeling rare, heterogeneous insurance claims and extracting signals from sparse, multi-epoch protostar observations.

112.name: Sascha Caron
discussion_points: How could Sascha's density-information-buffer VAEs/GANs be adapted to generate frequency- and instrument-aware synthetic multi-wavelength/multi-epoch images of protostellar disks, so Daniel can train DNNs and Siamese networks on realistic, label-rich datasets without running enormous numbers of radiative-transfer simulations?

Can the DeepXS-style ultra-fast surrogate approach be repurposed to emulate expensive radiative-transfer or hydrodynamic dust-evolution models, enabling active-learning-driven scans of high-dimensional disk parameter spaces (grain size distributions, turbulence, planet mass/location) in the early stages of Daniel's PhD?

Would anomaly-detection frameworks developed for LHC searches (ensemble One-Class DSVD + normalizing flows, DDD, mixture-of-theories training) help detect unexpected substructures or transient protostellar phenomena in heterogeneous observational campaigns, and how should we adapt their uncertainty quantification to avoid instrument/systematic-driven false positives?

How can Siamese and contrastive-network training be combined with transformer/graph architectures (used for tracking in collider data) to robustly match and track evolving disk features—gaps, spirals, clumps—across epochs and instruments, and what metrics should we use to quantify genuine physical evolution versus observational variability?

What would an open, reproducible benchmark/pipeline for protostar/disk ML look like if modeled on Dark Machines / SPOT / AutoSourceID—i.e., standardized synthetic+real datasets, uncertainty-calibration tasks, and low-latency/neuromorphic deployment targets for on-telescope pre-filtering—and how could we jointly seed such a resource for the community?
112.opening_line: We should explore adapting collider ML tools—fast, uncertainty-aware generative models and anomaly detectors—to protostellar disk observations.

26.name: Jerome Chenevez
discussion_points: Have we considered whether the time‑frequency and QPO detection techniques used on X‑ray burst lightcurves (e.g., wavelets, dynamic power spectra) could be combined with DNNs to characterize protostellar accretion variability — for example, training a CNN/transformer on spectro‑temporal representations of protostar time series to find low S/N or quasi‑periodic accretion signatures?

Could autoencoders be used not just for denoising but to create an interpretable latent space tying FITS image features to physical parameters (grain size distribution, disk inclination, inner rim location)? Jerome’s large catalogs and simulated reflection models could provide labels or constraints to help disentangle latent axes.

Would a Siamese/few‑shot network be effective for cross‑matching transient events or morphological substructures across instruments and epochs — e.g., learning a distance metric that recognizes the same disk gap or outburst signature in ALMA, NIR and archival mosaics despite different resolution and instrument systematics?

How can mosaicking and co‑addition practices from high‑energy missions (JEM‑X/INTEGRAL) inform building robust, multi‑epoch training sets for protostellar DNNs — specifically: handling FITS/WCS metadata, variable PSFs, exposure weighting, and synthetic augmentation to bridge domain gaps between simulations and observations?

Could we design physics‑informed network architectures (e.g., embedding a simple radiative transfer/reflection operator or conservation constraint into the loss) so that learned features map directly to interpretable disk/accretion physics — and as a testbed, compare signatures of disk instabilities in compact‑object accretion vs. protoplanetary disks?
26.opening_line: We should explore whether DNNs and autoencoders used on FITS‑based X‑ray timing and mosaics can reveal analogous transient accretion signatures and substructures in protostellar disks.

87.name: Clément Cherblamc
discussion_points: How could the U‑Net super‑resolution pipelines you use for polar remote‑sensing (Clément) be adapted to interferometric imaging of protoplanetary disks (Daniel) — e.g., handling ALMA’s uv‑coverage/PSF, complex noise, and using physics‑aware loss terms trained on radiative‑transfer synthetic observations?

Can we use autoencoders or VAEs to learn compact, interpretable latent spaces for multi‑scale substructures — rings, gaps, spirals in disks and spatial SMB patterns on ice sheets — and then use those latents for anomaly detection, morphometry, or generative augmentation?

Would Siamese/contrastive architectures help with sparse, multi‑epoch alignment problems both of you face: matching protostar/disk observations across instruments and time, and aligning satellite/reanalysis frames to detect subtle ice‑mass changes — what kinds of positive/negative pair sampling and augmentations would work?

What physics‑guided constraints (mass/energy conservation, radiative transfer priors, or surface‑process parametrizations) are most critical to impose on DNNs in each domain, and can we design loss functions or hybrid models (PINN + U‑Net/autoencoder) that are portable between climate and astrophysical imaging?

Given we’re both at Niels Bohr Institute, should we prototype a shared toolkit: simulator→augmenter→pretrained encoder library with evaluation metrics (multi‑scale reconstruction, calibration/uncertainty) to accelerate Daniel’s DNN start and let Clément test cross‑domain ideas — what datasets and benchmarks would we include first?
87.opening_line: We should explore applying U‑Net super‑resolution, autoencoders and contrastive methods to the shared challenge of reconstructing sparse, multi‑scale observational fields in both ice‑sheet and protoplanetary‑disk data.

31.name: Daniel Lomholt Christensen
discussion_points: Can we combine McStas-style neutron/instrument simulators and radiative-transfer forward models (e.g., RADMC-3D) to produce calibrated synthetic protostar/disk observations so autoencoders and siamese nets learn latent variables tied to physical generative parameters (grain-size distribution, accretion rate, instrument misalignment) rather than purely observational features?

Have you considered representing a protoplanetary disk or instrument geometry as a graph (nodes = annuli, grain populations, detectors; edges = transport, scattering, coupling) and using GNNs—similar to transport/geometry problems in instrument simulation—to model dust dynamics or approximate scattering kernels?

Since you are both focused on 'what made the datasets', would simulation-based inference (neural posterior/likelihood estimators, differentiable surrogates) be a promising route to invert instrument-convolved observations and obtain calibrated posteriors on physical parameters, and could we co-develop surrogate models to speed up expensive forward sims?

How could we combine autoencoders and siamese architectures to (a) learn a compact manifold of multi-epoch/multi-wavelength protostellar observations, (b) disentangle instrumental/calibration variations from true astrophysical evolution, and (c) flag anomalous substructures for targeted follow-up?

Given small real-data regimes, which sim-to-real strategies would you prioritize—domain randomization, physics-informed priors, uncertainty-aware/Bayesian DNNs, or active learning—and can instrument simulations be used to generate principled domain shifts for stress-testing transfer and quantifying uncertainty?
31.opening_line: We should explore simulation-informed neural models to uncover the generative physics behind our instruments and protostellar observations.

49.name: Hans Christiansen
discussion_points: Autoencoders as physics‑aware compressors: could we train autoencoders on radiative‑transfer simulations of protoplanetary disks (conditioned on grain size, turbulence, inclination) to produce low‑dimensional, interpretable latents — and can Hans' experience with volumetric imaging pipelines and simulated data help design loss terms or regularizers that enforce radiative/energy conservation or known scaling laws?

Siamese/contrastive networks for temporal matching and proper‑motion inference: can we use Siamese architectures to match substructures across multi‑epoch or multiwavelength observations (detecting migrating clumps or evolving rings), borrowing ideas from contrastive representations used in other tracking problems and from Hans' image‑fusion registration workflows to robustly register and compare observations?

Simulation→real domain adaptation and calibrated uncertainty: how can we combine deep networks with Bayesian recalibration (PAINTOR‑style or hierarchical Bayesian posteriors) so that parameter estimates from models trained on simulations have trustworthy error bars on real telescope data — and could Hans' experience with Bayesian prioritization and causal‑variant calibration inform strategy for posterior correction and priors?

Generative benchmarks and community datasets: would it be productive to co‑develop an open, annotated suite of simulated disk images (varying dust physics, substructure types, noise/PSF) using conditional generative models, plus an open pipeline for fusing multiwavelength stacks (inspired by Hans' 3D Slicer workflow), so experimentalists and ML newcomers (like Daniel) have standard training/validation sets?

Unsupervised discovery of ‘phases’ or morphology classes: can unsupervised manifold learning, clustering in latent space, or topological data analysis—techniques used to find phases in strongly correlated systems—be adapted to automatically discover and interpret disk substructure classes (rings vs spirals vs vortices), and how would we link latent features back to physical quantities such as dust‑to‑gas ratio or local turbulence?
49.opening_line: We should explore how simulation‑trained deep models plus Bayesian prioritization can connect protoplanetary‑disk imaging and condensed‑matter inference.

78.name: Francesca Curbis
discussion_points: Compare how autoencoders (bottleneck compression, denoising, latent-space anomaly detection) could be applied to both Ce:YAG / MCP / spectrometer images from accelerators and multi-epoch protostellar images — what architecture choices, loss functions (e.g., perceptual vs. physics-conserving), and latent-space interpretability would be most useful for preserving physics (flux, PSF, coherence)?

Exchange strategies for sim-to-real / domain adaptation: both of you rely heavily on simulations (GENESIS / start‑to‑end for FELs; radiative transfer / MCRT for disks). Discuss concrete approaches — cycleGAN, domain-adaptive fine-tuning, physics-informed losses or calibrated forward models — and propose a benchmark task (synthetic→real) to evaluate transfer methods across the two domains.

Explore Siamese / contrastive networks for cross-epoch matching and morphological similarity: Daniel could use them to link features across observations (e.g., moving clumps, rings, gaps), while Francesca could use the same idea to detect subtle changes in beam profiles or align diagnostics across detectors — talk about suitable data augmentations, distance metrics, and evaluation criteria for low-SNR, high-dynamic-range images.

Discuss uncertainty quantification and interpretability requirements for scientific deployment: compare methods (ensembles, Bayesian NNs, evidential deep learning, calibrated predictors) and how to present uncertainties to instrument/control systems (real-time beam tuning vs. cataloguing protostellar substructures), and whether disentangled/physically-structured latent spaces could map to meaningful parameters (grain size, eccentricity, emittance, energy spread).

Propose small, concrete collaborative projects leveraging regional resources: e.g., build a shared synthetic/real paired dataset and run a 2‑day hackathon to adapt an autoencoder pipeline for both datasets; organize short lab visits to swap knowledge about high-frame-rate detectors, timing jitter mitigation, and pre-processing pipelines; or co-develop a surrogate model to replace expensive forward sims for faster inference in both accelerator and disk modelling.
78.opening_line: We should compare autoencoder and sim‑to‑real strategies used for accelerator diagnostics and protostellar imaging to find common ML building blocks.
